teile.einleitung: The second law of thermodynamics is one of the most important laws of nature in physics. Put simply, it says that disorder, called entropy, increases over time in an isolated system. It explains why hot tea cools down and why a bedroom does not tidy itself.
wichtigste: The second law says that entropy increases over time in an isolated system.
Put simply, entropy is a measure of disorder.
Heat flows by itself only from a warmer to a colder body.
It was formulated mainly by Rudolf Clausius, who taught in Zurich for a long time.
It shows that a perpetual motion machine is impossible.
It explains why many processes only run in one direction.

abschnitte.text: **Thermodynamics**, the science of heat, is a part of physics. It studies heat, energy and how they change from one form into another. The first law says that energy is never lost, but only changes its form. The second law says in which **direction** such changes happen by themselves.

**Entropy** is a physical quantity that is described simply as a measure of disorder. More precisely, it tells you in how many ways the particles of a system can be arranged. In an isolated system, which exchanges neither energy nor matter, it cannot decrease. That is why everything tends by itself towards an evenly spread state.

A hot cup of tea cools down in a room, but never gets hot again by itself. An ice cube in a glass of juice melts until everything has the same temperature. A drop of ink spreads out in water, but never gathers back into a drop on its own. And a child’s bedroom tends to get untidy, whereas tidying up costs **energy**.

In 1850 the German physicist **Rudolf Clausius** stated that heat cannot pass by itself from a colder to a warmer body. From 1855 to 1867 he taught at the Polytechnic in Zurich, today’s ETH. During his time in Zurich, in 1865, he introduced the term **entropy**. Earlier, in 1824, the Frenchman Sadi Carnot had laid important foundations on the efficiency of steam engines.

The second law shows that no machine can turn heat completely into work. Some is always lost to the surroundings as waste heat, for example in a car engine. A machine that runs for ever and does work at the same time, a **perpetual motion machine**, is therefore impossible. A fridge can make it colder inside, but it needs electricity to do so and gives off heat at the back.

The Austrian **Ludwig Boltzmann** explained entropy through the movement of countless particles and probability. Disordered states are simply far more likely than ordered ones. Because entropy increases, many processes only run in one direction; this is called the **arrow of time**. That is why you notice straight away when a film of a glass breaking is played backwards.

begriffe.erklaerung: A measure of how disordered or evenly spread out a system is.
An area that exchanges neither energy nor matter with its surroundings.
An imaginary machine that would run for ever without any supply of energy.
The part of physics that deals with heat and energy.

gewusst: Living things build up order, but only because they take in energy and in doing so make their surroundings all the more disordered.
Ludwig Boltzmann’s famous formula for entropy is written on his gravestone in Vienna.
Some researchers think that the universe might end in a state of maximum entropy in the distant future.

teile.einleitung: Active noise cancelling is a technique that cancels out disturbing noise with anti-noise. Headphones with this feature produce a sound that is exactly the opposite of the noise. Together the two sound waves add up to almost silence.
wichtigste: Active noise cancelling is based on destructive interference.
A microphone picks up the disturbing noise.
The anti-noise is shifted in phase by 180 degrees so that the waves cancel each other out.
The technique works best with low, steady noises.
High sounds are blocked mainly by the passive insulation of the ear cushions.
There is a feedforward method and a feedback method.
Active noise cancelling is also used in aeroplane cabins and cars.

abschnitte.text: Noise is a sound wave that makes the air vibrate back and forth. In **active noise cancelling** a device deliberately produces a second sound wave. It is calculated so that it cancels out the noise. The technique is known as Active Noise Cancelling, or **ANC** for short.

When two waves meet, they overlap; this is called **interference**. If a wave crest meets a wave trough exactly, they cancel each other out. For this, the anti-noise must be **shifted in phase by 180 degrees** compared with the noise. This cancelling out is called **destructive interference**. You can imagine it like two children pulling on a rope equally hard in opposite directions.

A **microphone** in the headphones picks up the disturbing noise. A small chip calculates the matching anti-noise in fractions of a second, and the speaker plays it. In the **feedforward method** the microphone sits on the outside and measures the noise before it reaches the ear. In the **feedback method** it sits inside the ear cup near the speaker and checks what actually arrives. Good headphones combine both methods.

The technique works best with low, steady noises such as the hum of aircraft engines or trains. Such waves are long and easy to predict. High and sudden sounds, such as voices or clinking, are harder to cancel out. Here it is mainly the passive insulation of the ear cushions that does the blocking. That is why you can often still hear quiet conversations with such headphones.

The idea is old: the German physicist **Paul Lueg** applied for a patent for it in the 1930s. The technique only became usable, however, with fast electronics. Pilots were the first to use it, to protect their hearing in the noisy cockpit. Today it is found in many headphones and is also used in aeroplane cabins and cars.

begriffe.erklaerung: The overlapping of two or more waves.
Tells you at which point in its vibration a wave is at a given moment.
A sound wave that copies a noise exactly in mirror image.
Protection from noise by material, for example thick ear cushions.

gewusst: Two loud noises can add up to almost silence.
Some headphones have a transparency mode that deliberately lets outside sounds back in.
The idea of anti-noise was patented long before there were portable headphones.

teile.einleitung: Alpha decay is a kind of radioactive decay in which a heavy atomic nucleus ejects an alpha particle. In the process the nucleus turns into a different element. The process can only be explained with quantum physics and the astonishing tunnel effect.
wichtigste: In alpha decay a nucleus gives off a helium nucleus made of two protons and two neutrons.
Alpha decay occurs mainly in heavy nuclei.
Alpha decay turns radium-226 into radon-222.
The alpha particle leaves the nucleus thanks to the quantum mechanical tunnel effect.
Alpha particles typically have an energy of a few MeV.
The energy spectrum of a nuclide consists of sharp, discrete lines.
The Geiger-Nuttall rule says: the greater the energy of the alpha particles, the shorter the half-life.

abschnitte.text: In alpha decay an unstable nucleus ejects an **alpha particle**, that is two protons and two neutrons. As a result the atomic number falls by 2 and the mass number by 4. In this way, for example, **radium-226** becomes the noble gas **radon-222**. Alpha decay occurs mainly in heavy nuclei such as uranium, thorium, radium and polonium.

Inside the nucleus the strong nuclear force holds the particles together. Seen from outside, the nucleus is surrounded by an electrical repulsion, the **Coulomb barrier**. Strictly speaking the alpha particle has too little energy to get over this wall. According to quantum physics, however, it can slip through with a small probability, as if it were taking a tunnel through a mountain. George Gamow found this explanation through the **tunnel effect** in 1928.

Alpha particles from natural decays usually have an energy of a few **MeV**, that is millions of electronvolts. For a particular nuclide they always have precisely fixed energies. Their spectrum therefore consists of sharp, discrete lines. Because the alpha particle is much lighter than the remaining nucleus, it gets most of the kinetic energy. In the decay of radium-226 it is around 98 per cent; the rest goes to the new nucleus as **recoil**.

The **half-life** is the time after which half of the nuclei have decayed. It varies greatly among alpha emitters: uranium-238 has a half-life of about 4.5 billion years, radium-226 of around 1600 years. In 1911 Hans Geiger and John Nuttall discovered a connection, the **Geiger-Nuttall rule**. The greater the energy of the alpha particles, the shorter the half-life.

Often the new nucleus is itself radioactive again and decays further. This produces whole **decay chains**, in which alpha and beta decays alternate. Thorium-232 decays through such a chain to stable lead-208. This chain contains exactly 6 alpha decays. Geologists also use such chains to work out the age of rocks.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particular kind of atomic nucleus with a fixed number of protons and neutrons.
A quantum effect by which particles get through a barrier even though their energy is really not enough to do so.
The time in which half of the radioactive nuclei decay.
Megaelectronvolt, a unit of energy for very small particles.

gewusst: The radon found in some cellars is produced by the alpha decay of radium in the ground.
Some alpha emitters decay in fractions of a second, others take billions of years.
Alpha decay was one of the first processes that could be explained with quantum physics.

teile.einleitung: The stopping distance is the whole distance a vehicle travels from the moment a danger is spotted until it comes to a standstill. It is made up of the reaction distance and the braking distance. If you understand it, you understand why speed and attention are so important in traffic.
wichtigste: The stopping distance is made up of the reaction distance and the braking distance.
The reaction distance is the distance you travel before you even brake.
The reaction distance does not depend on the brakes or the state of the road.
The braking distance increases with the square of the speed.
Twice the speed means roughly four times the braking distance.
On wet or icy roads the braking distance becomes much longer.
Distraction, for example by a mobile phone, makes the reaction distance longer.

abschnitte.text: When a driver sees a danger, first the **reaction time** passes, usually about one second. During this time the car carries on without braking; this is the **reaction distance**. Only after that does the **braking distance** begin, until the car stands still. Both together give the stopping distance. If the reaction distance is 14 m and the braking distance 12 m, the stopping distance is 26 m.

You calculate the reaction distance as speed times reaction time. For the braking distance the formula is v² divided by twice the **deceleration**. A car at 72 km/h travels 20 m per second. With a reaction time of 1 s and a deceleration of 10 m/s², that gives 20 m plus 20 m, so a stopping distance of 40 m. At 120 km/h and 8 m/s² it is already around 103 m, as long as a football pitch.

How strongly a car can brake depends on the tyres, the brakes and the road. On dry tarmac a car manages about 8 to 10 m/s². On a wet road it is often only 4 m/s², and on snow and ice much less still. At 20 m/s and a reaction time of 1 s, the stopping distance on a wet road increases to 70 m. That is why you should drive more slowly in the rain and keep a bigger gap.

If a child jumps onto the road 15 m in front of a car, every kilometre per hour counts. With a reaction time of 1 s and a deceleration of 8 m/s², a car at 30 km/h just manages to stop in time. At 50 km/h the car is still heading towards that spot almost without braking during that time. That is why many Swiss residential areas have **30 km/h zones** and shared zones.

If you look at your phone, you react much later. If the reaction time at 36 km/h goes up from 1 s to 2 s, the stopping distance becomes 10 m longer. Tiredness and alcohol also make the reaction time much longer. For children this means: cars cannot stop immediately, even if they seem to be going slowly. At a **zebra crossing** you should therefore wait until the vehicles have really stopped.

begriffe.erklaerung: The time between spotting a danger and pressing the brake.
The distance you still travel during the reaction time.
The distance from starting to brake until coming to a standstill.
How strongly a vehicle slows down when braking, measured in m/s².

gewusst: At 50 km/h a car travels almost 14 m in one second of reaction time.
With the same braking force, a car at 50 km/h has a braking distance almost three times as long as one at 30 km/h.
Driving schools teach a rule of thumb: the braking distance in metres is roughly the speed divided by 10, multiplied by itself.

teile.einleitung: An ammeter is a measuring instrument used to measure electric current. It shows how many amperes are flowing through a circuit. For it to measure correctly, it has to be connected into the circuit in a particular way.
wichtigste: An ammeter is used to measure electric current.
The reading is given in amperes or milliamperes.
An ammeter is connected in series in the circuit.
It has a very small internal resistance so that it hardly obstructs the current.
Today the ammeter is usually part of a multimeter.
With a clamp meter you can measure current without opening the circuit.
Connected wrongly, an ammeter can cause a short circuit.

abschnitte.text: An **ammeter** shows how strong the electric current in a circuit is. The name is made up of ampere and the Greek word for measuring. There are instruments with a needle and scale and instruments with a digital display. It shows small currents in milliamperes and large ones in amperes. There are often several **measuring ranges** that you can switch between.

An ammeter must be connected in **series**. This means you break the circuit and put the instrument in the gap, so that all the current flows through it. So that it does not distort the measurement, it has a very small **internal resistance**. A voltmeter for voltage, on the other hand, is connected in parallel. Anyone who accidentally connects an ammeter in parallel across a battery causes a short circuit.

Older instruments often work with a **moving-coil movement**. In it the current flows through a small coil of wire between the poles of a magnet. The current turns the coil itself into a magnet, so that it turns and moves the needle. The stronger the current, the further the needle swings. Digital instruments, on the other hand, measure the voltage across a very small resistor and calculate the current from it.

Today people usually use a **multimeter**, which can measure current, voltage and resistance. You choose what is to be measured with a rotary switch. Electricians often use a **clamp meter**. It is simply placed round a cable and measures the magnetic field produced by the current. That way you do not have to break the circuit.

At school you build simple circuits with a battery, a small bulb and an ammeter. This shows you, for example, that the same current flows everywhere in a series circuit. In a parallel circuit, on the other hand, the current divides. It is important to start with the largest measuring range so that the instrument is not overloaded. Work on mains sockets is off limits for pupils.

begriffe.erklaerung: A circuit in which all the components lie one after another in the same current path.
The resistance of a measuring instrument itself.
A measuring instrument for current, voltage and resistance.
A direct connection between two terminals, through which a very large current flows.

gewusst: The first instruments for measuring current used a compass needle that was deflected by the current in the wire.
A clamp meter measures the current without touching the cable.
Many multimeters have their own small fuse built in for measuring current.

teile.einleitung: The state of matter describes the form in which a substance exists: solid, liquid or gas. With water you can easily observe all three states, as ice, as liquid water and as water vapour. Whether a substance is solid, liquid or a gas depends mainly on the temperature.
wichtigste: The three most important states of matter are solid, liquid and gas.
Water exists as ice, as liquid water and as water vapour.
Whether a substance is solid, liquid or a gas depends on temperature and pressure.
Water melts at 0 degrees Celsius and boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.
The changes are called, for example, melting, freezing, evaporating and condensing.
The particle model explains the states well.
A fourth state is plasma, found for example in lightning and in the sun.

abschnitte.text: A **solid** substance such as ice or stone has a fixed shape and a fixed volume. A **liquid** such as water or milk has a fixed volume, but takes the shape of its container. A **gas** such as air or water vapour has neither a fixed shape nor a fixed volume and spreads out through the whole space. Depending on the temperature, the same substance can exist in all three states.

All substances are made of tiny particles. In a solid the particles sit close together in an orderly way and only wobble in their places. In a liquid they are also close together, but can slide past each other. In a gas the particles fly quickly through the space, far apart from each other. The warmer a substance is, the more strongly its particles move.

When ice is warmed, it **melts** into water; when water cools, it **freezes** into ice. When water is heated, it **evaporates**, and on a cold window pane the vapour condenses back into drops. Some substances change directly from solid to gas; this is called sublimation. The opposite change is called deposition, and that is how hoar frost forms on cold winter days. Washing also dries in frosty weather, because the ice in it sublimates.

Water only boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level. In the mountains the air pressure is lower, so water boils there at a lower temperature. On the Jungfraujoch at around 3450 metres it already boils at below 90 degrees. That is why pasta takes longer to cook there. A **pressure cooker**, on the other hand, raises the pressure, so that water gets hotter than 100 degrees and food cooks faster.

Most substances shrink as they cool. Water is an exception: it is densest at 4 degrees Celsius and expands when it freezes. That is why **ice** floats on water and lakes freeze from the top. In this way fish can survive the winter at the bottom of the lake. This property is called the **anomaly of water**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The form in which a substance exists: solid, liquid or gas.
The change from gas to liquid, for example on steamed-up windows.
The direct change from solid to gas.
The temperature at which a liquid starts to boil.
A very hot gas that conducts electricity, often called the fourth state of matter.

gewusst: Dry ice, made of frozen carbon dioxide, never becomes liquid but turns directly into gas.
Because water expands when it freezes, full glass bottles can burst in the freezer.
Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature.

teile.einleitung: Sugar is a sweet-tasting substance that we know mainly as white crystals from the kitchen. Chemically it belongs to the carbohydrates, which living things use as a source of energy. It is also fascinating how sugar dissolves in water and turns into caramel when heated.
wichtigste: The chemical name for table sugar is sucrose, and it is obtained from sugar beet or sugar cane.
Sugar dissolves well in water, but not in cooking oil.
A liquid in which sugar is completely dissolved is called a solution.
Stirring and warm water help sugar to dissolve faster.
Fine icing sugar dissolves faster than coarse sugar grains.
If you keep adding more sugar to water, at some point some is left lying on the bottom.
If you heat sugar strongly in a pan, caramel forms.

abschnitte.text: In everyday life **sugar** usually means table sugar, chemically called **sucrose**. It is made of two smaller sugar building blocks, glucose and fructose. In chemistry all these substances count as **carbohydrates**. Plants make sugar during photosynthesis with the help of sunlight.

Worldwide, sugar is mainly obtained from **sugar cane**, a tall grass from warm countries. In Europe, on the other hand, people use **sugar beet**. In Switzerland sugar beet is processed in the factories in Aarberg in the canton of Bern and in Frauenfeld in Thurgau. There the beet is sliced, the sweet juice is extracted, thickened and dried into crystals.

If you put sugar in water, the crystals slowly disappear, but the sugar is still there, because the water tastes sweet. The sugar particles spread out between the water particles and a **solution** forms. **Stirring**, warm water and fine sugar such as icing sugar speed up dissolving. In cooking oil, however, sugar does not dissolve; the grains simply stay where they are.

Water can only take up a certain amount of sugar, even though this amount is surprisingly large. At room temperature around two kilograms of sugar dissolve in one litre of water. Once this limit is reached, it is called a **saturated solution**, and any more sugar stays on the bottom. Even more sugar dissolves in hot water, which is used when making syrup.

If you heat sugar strongly in a pan, it first melts into a clear liquid. With more heat it turns golden yellow to brown and **caramel** forms with its typical smell. In the process the sugar molecules change chemically. If the sugar gets too hot, it burns and tastes bitter, so care is needed when caramelising, because hot sugar causes bad burns.

Sugar gives the body energy quickly; the brain and muscles especially need it. Too much sugar, however, can lead to being overweight and to tooth decay. The World Health Organization recommends eating only a little added sugar. A lot of sugar is hidden in fizzy drinks, ketchup or breakfast cereals, so it is worth looking at the list of ingredients.

begriffe.erklaerung: The chemical name for table sugar.
Nutrients such as sugar and starch that give the body energy.
A liquid in which another substance is completely dissolved.
A solution in which no more of a substance can dissolve.
A brown, aromatic substance that forms when sugar is heated strongly.

gewusst: At room temperature you can dissolve about twice as much sugar in a litre of water as the water itself weighs.
A sugar beet contains only about one sixth of its weight in sugar.
If you let a saturated sugar solution evaporate slowly, large sugar crystals grow, known as rock sugar.

teile.einleitung: Most substances shrink as they cool and become denser. Water is an exception: it is densest at about 4 °C and even expands when it freezes. This anomaly of water makes ice float and lets fish survive the winter.
wichtigste: Water is densest at about 4 °C.
If you cool water from 4 °C to 1 °C, its volume increases.
When water freezes, its volume increases by about 9 per cent.
Ice has a density of about 0.92 g/cm³ and therefore floats on water.
A lake freezes from the surface downwards.
At the bottom of a deep frozen lake the water is about 4 °C.
Water freezing in rock cracks splits the rock apart; this is called frost shattering.

abschnitte.text: **Anomaly** means a departure from the rule. Almost all substances become denser as they cool and denser still as a solid. Water, on the other hand, only becomes denser down to about 4 °C. If it cools further, it expands again. When it freezes, it suddenly gets about 9 per cent bigger, and at 0.92 g/cm³ ice is lighter than liquid water.

The reason lies in **hydrogen bonds**. These are weak bonds between water molecules. In ice these bonds arrange the molecules in a regular **crystal lattice** with many empty spaces. That is why ice takes up more room than liquid water. Even shortly before freezing, small groups like this form, which is why water already expands below 4 °C.

In winter a lake cools from the top. Water at 4 °C, being the heaviest water, sinks to the bottom. Colder water stays at the top and finally freezes into a layer of ice. The ice acts like an **insulating layer** and protects the water below from cooling further. In this way fish and other animals survive the winter, even in mountain lakes such as Lake Sils in the Engadine, which freezes over every winter.

When water gets into cracks in rocks and freezes, it expands and presses with great force. Over time this breaks the rock apart; this is called **frost shattering**. In the Alps this creates slopes of scree below rock faces. Roads also get potholes in winter when water gets into cracks and freezes. Water pipes and glass bottles can burst in frosty weather.

Because ice is slightly lighter than water, only about a tenth of an iceberg sticks out of the sea. Most of it lies invisible below the surface, which is where the saying “the tip of the iceberg” comes from. Only a few other substances behave like water. One example is the metal **gallium**, whose solid form floats on its melt. Bismuth and silicon also expand when they solidify.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much mass there is in a certain volume, for example grams per cubic centimetre.
A departure from normal behaviour.
A weak attraction between water molecules.
The breaking of rock by water freezing in cracks.

gewusst: Without the anomaly, lakes would freeze from the bottom up and many animals would die in winter.
A full glass bottle in the freezer can burst because the water needs more room when it freezes.
The metal gallium melts at only around 30 °C and can turn liquid in a warm hand.

teile.einleitung: In additive colour mixing, new colours are made by laying coloured light on top of each other. Almost all colours can be mixed from red, green and blue, and together they make white. This is exactly how every screen conjures up its colourful pictures.
wichtigste: The three primary colours of additive colour mixing are red, green and blue.
If you mix all three equally bright, you get white.
If none of the three lamps is on, you see black.
Green and blue light together make cyan.
The mixing is called additive because light is added and the mixture gets brighter.
In 1853 Hermann Grassmann described the laws of additive colour mixing.
Screens use additive colour mixing; there, orange is made from a lot of red, some green and no blue.

abschnitte.text: In additive colour mixing, lights of different colours are mixed together. The three **primary colours** are red, green and blue, abbreviated **RGB**. Each extra light makes the mixture brighter. That is why it is called additive, from the Latin word for adding. If no light shines at all, it stays black.

Red and green together make yellow. Green and blue make **cyan**, a bright turquoise blue. Red and blue make **magenta**, a strong pink. All three together make white. If you change the brightness of the three lights, millions of other shades are created.

In our retina there are three kinds of **cones**, sense cells for colour. One kind reacts mainly to red light, one to green and one to blue. The brain compares the signals and creates the impression of colour from them. That is why mixing just these three colours is enough to fake almost any colour.

Mobile phones, televisions and computer screens are made up of millions of tiny dots, the **pixels**. Each pixel has a red, a green and a blue part, each of which can shine brighter or darker. From a distance they merge in the eye into one colour. For orange, for example, there is a lot of red, some green and no blue. Stage spotlights and coloured LED lamps also mix their colours in this way.

In the 17th century Isaac Newton already showed that white light is made up of all colours. In 1853 the German mathematician **Hermann Grassmann** described the laws of additive colour mixing. In 1861 the Scottish physicist **James Clerk Maxwell** showed one of the first colour pictures. To do so, he projected red, green and blue partial images of a tartan ribbon on top of each other.

With coloured pencils and watercolours mixing works differently. There each colour swallows part of the light, so the mixture gets darker. This is called **subtractive colour mixing**. Printers work this way with cyan, magenta, yellow and black.

begriffe.erklaerung: Short for red, green and blue, the primary colours of light.
A tiny dot of an image on a screen.
Sense cells in the eye with which we see colours.
Mixing of dyes or paints in which the mixture gets darker.

gewusst: Yellow on a screen contains no yellow light at all, only red and green.
With a magnifying glass you can make out the little red, green and blue dots of light on many screens.
White light on a mobile phone screen is made when all three colour dots shine at full strength.

teile.einleitung: Alessandro Volta was an Italian physicist who invented the world’s first battery around 1800. His voltaic pile was the first to supply a steady electric current. The unit of electrical voltage, the volt, is named after him.
wichtigste: Alessandro Volta came from Italy and was born in Como in 1745.
Around 1800 he invented the voltaic pile, the first usable battery.
He was inspired by Luigi Galvani’s experiments with frogs’ legs.
In 1801 he demonstrated his invention to Napoleon.
He discovered the gas methane in a marsh.
The unit volt is named after him and gives the electrical voltage.
A normal socket in Switzerland has 230 volts.

abschnitte.text: Alessandro Volta was born in 1745 in **Como** on Lake Como, not far from the Swiss border at Chiasso. Even as a young man he was fascinated by electricity. Later he became professor of physics at the University of **Pavia**. He died in 1827 in his home town of Como.

In 1775 Volta improved the **electrophorus**, a device with which you can produce and store electric charge. In 1776 he studied gas bubbles rising from the mud of a marsh on Lake Maggiore. In doing so he discovered the flammable gas **methane**. He even built a kind of pistol in which an electric spark set the gas alight.

The doctor Luigi Galvani from Bologna had observed that frogs’ legs twitch when touched with two different metals. Galvani believed that the electricity came from the animal itself. Volta disagreed and suspected that the current was produced by the contact between the two metals. To prove this, he carried on researching and in doing so invented the battery.

Around 1800 Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper alternately on top of each other. Between them he put pieces of cardboard or cloth soaked in salt water. This tower, the **voltaic pile**, supplied a lasting electric current for the first time. In 1801 Volta demonstrated his invention to **Napoleon** in Paris, who later made him a count.

The voltaic pile was the starting point for the study of electric current. Shortly afterwards researchers used it to split water into hydrogen and oxygen. In Volta’s honour the unit of electrical voltage is called the **volt**. The number of volts on a battery gives its voltage; a socket in Switzerland has 230 volts. In Como the Tempio Voltiano museum commemorates the famous scientist.

begriffe.erklaerung: The push that makes electric current flow, measured in volts.
The first battery, a stack of metal discs and soaked cardboard.
An old device for producing electric charge.
A flammable gas that forms, for example, in marshes.

gewusst: Volta’s portrait used to be on the Italian 10,000 lire note.
Volta’s name is on every device that has a voltage given in volts.
You can even build a simple battery with a lemon, a copper coin and a galvanised nail.

teile.einleitung: Antimatter is the mirror image of ordinary matter. For every particle there is an antiparticle with the same mass but the opposite charge. When matter and antimatter meet, they disappear and turn into pure energy.
wichtigste: With his equation for the electron, Paul Dirac predicted the positron.
Carl D. Anderson detected the positron in cosmic rays in 1932.
When an electron and a positron meet, they usually annihilate into gamma photons.
An antiproton has a negative elementary charge.
In 1995 antihydrogen atoms were made for the first time at CERN.
Positron emission tomography (PET) in hospitals uses positrons.
Why there is almost only matter in the universe is an unsolved mystery.

abschnitte.text: Every particle has an **antiparticle**. The antiparticle of the electron is called the **positron** and is positively charged. The antiproton, on the other hand, is negatively charged. An antihydrogen atom can be built from an antiproton and a positron. Antimatter has the same mass as normal matter.

In 1928 the British physicist **Paul Dirac** set up an equation for fast electrons. It followed from it that there had to be a positively charged counterpart. In 1932 the American **Carl D. Anderson** actually found this positron in cosmic rays. Both received a Nobel Prize for this. In 1955 the antiproton was also discovered in California.

When matter and antimatter meet, they destroy each other. This **annihilation** turns all their mass into energy, usually into gamma radiation. According to Einstein’s formula E = m · c², 1 g of antimatter and 1 g of matter give around 1.8 · 10^14 joules. That is about as much electricity as a large nuclear power station such as Gösgen supplies in about two days. Unfortunately, making antimatter costs far more energy than you get back.

**CERN** near Geneva is the most important centre for antimatter research. In 1995 a few antihydrogen atoms were made there for the first time. Today the Antiproton Decelerator slows antiprotons down so that researchers can catch them in **magnetic traps**. In 2023 the ALPHA-g experiment showed that antihydrogen falls downwards in a gravitational field just like normal matter. Altogether only tiny amounts have been made so far, much less than a millionth of a gram.

In hospitals antimatter is used in **positron emission tomography**, PET for short. Patients are injected with a weakly radioactive substance that gives off positrons. The positrons immediately annihilate with electrons in the body. The resulting gamma rays are measured and show, for example, where tumours are.

In the Big Bang equal numbers of particles and antiparticles should really have been created. Today, however, the universe consists almost entirely of matter. Where the antimatter has gone is one of the biggest open questions in physics. Researchers at CERN are looking for tiny differences between matter and antimatter that could explain this.

begriffe.erklaerung: A particle with the same mass as a normal particle but the opposite charge.
The antiparticle of the electron, positively charged.
The mutual destruction of a particle and an antiparticle, which produces energy.
A large European research centre for particle physics near Geneva.

gewusst: Bananas contain radioactive potassium and therefore now and then give off tiny amounts of positrons.
Antihydrogen cannot be kept in a normal bottle, because it would immediately annihilate with the walls.
Positrons are sometimes produced in thunderstorms too, as satellites have measured.

teile.einleitung: The amplitude is the greatest displacement of an oscillation or wave from its rest position. It tells you how strongly something is vibrating. With sound, the amplitude determines how loud a note is.
wichtigste: The amplitude is the greatest displacement from the rest position.
The rest position is the position in which a vibrating body would be at rest.
The greater the amplitude of a sound wave, the louder the sound.
The pitch of a note does not depend on the amplitude, but on the frequency.
If the amplitude gets smaller over time, it is called a damped oscillation.
On an oscilloscope you can see the amplitude from the height of the curve.
The further you are from the sound source, the smaller the amplitude and the quieter the sound.

abschnitte.text: Everything that swings back and forth has a **rest position**, the position in which it would stand still. The **amplitude** is the greatest distance from this rest position. If a pendulum swings 10 cm to the left and 10 cm to the right, the amplitude is 10 cm. So you only measure from the middle to the outermost point, not from the far left to the far right.

Sound is a vibration of the air. The greater the amplitude of this vibration, the **louder** we hear the sound. The pitch, on the other hand, depends on the **frequency**, that is how often per second something vibrates. If you pluck a guitar string harder, the note gets louder but not higher. Loudness is measured in **decibels**.

A pendulum or a swing does not keep swinging for ever. Because of friction and air resistance, the amplitude gets a little smaller with every swing. This is called a **damped oscillation**. A gong that has been struck also slowly gets quieter, because its amplitude decreases. Shock absorbers in a car deliberately make vibrations stop quickly.

With an **oscilloscope** you can show vibrations as a curve on a screen. The height of the curve shows the amplitude, and the distance between the wave crests shows the frequency. Music programs on a computer also show sounds as a waveform. You can recognise loud parts by high peaks and quiet parts by flat ones.

Water waves also have an amplitude: it is roughly the height of a wave crest above the calm water level. During earthquakes **seismographs** record the amplitude of the ground vibrations. From this, experts calculate the strength of the earthquake. In Switzerland this is done by the Swiss Seismological Service at ETH Zurich.

begriffe.erklaerung: The position in which a vibrating body stands still when nothing pushes it.
How many vibrations take place per second, measured in hertz.
The gradual shrinking of an oscillation.
A measuring instrument that shows vibrations as a curve on a screen.

gewusst: A whisper and a scream can have exactly the same pitch; they differ only in amplitude.
If you move twice as far from a sound source, the amplitude roughly halves in open space.
Radio used to have amplitude modulation, AM for short, in which the music was carried in the amplitude of the radio wave.

teile.einleitung: Mass-energy equivalence says that mass and energy can be turned into each other. In 1905 Albert Einstein summed this up in the famous formula E = mc². Even a tiny amount of mass corresponds to a huge amount of energy.
wichtigste: Albert Einstein’s formula E = mc² describes how mass and energy can be turned into each other.
E stands for energy, m for mass and c for the speed of light.
The speed of light is around 300,000 kilometres per second.
Einstein published the idea in 1905, when he was working at the patent office in Bern.
Because c² is huge, a small amount of mass contains a great deal of energy.
The sun shines because it turns mass into energy through nuclear fusion.
Nuclear power stations also use this relationship.

abschnitte.text: In the formula **E = mc²**, E stands for energy, m for mass and c for the **speed of light**. The small sign ² means that c is multiplied by itself. The speed of light is about 300,000 kilometres per second, and squared that is an enormous number. That is why just one gram of mass corresponds to around 25 million kilowatt hours of energy. That is enough to supply several thousand Swiss households with electricity for a whole year.

**Albert Einstein** was born in Ulm in 1879 and later went to school in Aarau. He studied at ETH Zurich and from 1902 worked at the Federal Patent Office in Bern. There, in 1905, he published several ground-breaking papers, which is why it is called his miracle year. They included the **special theory of relativity** and, shortly afterwards, the derivation of E = mc². His former flat on the Kramgasse in Bern is now the Einstein House.

In the **sun**, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium nuclei; this is called **nuclear fusion**. The helium produced is slightly lighter than the hydrogen was before. The missing mass is released as energy and reaches us as light and heat. In this way the sun loses more than 4 million tonnes of mass every second. Even so, it is so big that it will go on shining for billions of years.

In **nuclear fission**, too, a small part of the mass is turned into energy. Heavy atomic nuclei such as uranium are split into smaller pieces. In nuclear power stations this energy heats water, and the steam drives turbines. In Switzerland such power stations are located, for example, in Gösgen, Leibstadt and Beznau. Sadly, the same physics was also used for atomic bombs.

The formula really always applies, even when we do not notice it. A charged battery, for example, is minimally heavier than a flat one. The difference, however, is so tiny that no scales can measure it. The other way round, mass can also be created from energy; this happens in large **particle accelerators** such as at CERN near Geneva. There, collisions create new particles from kinetic energy.

begriffe.erklaerung: The speed of light, around 300,000 kilometres per second.
The joining of light atomic nuclei, which releases energy.
The splitting of heavy atomic nuclei, which releases energy.
Einstein’s theory about space, time, mass and energy.

gewusst: Einstein did not receive the Nobel Prize in 1921 for E = mc², but for his explanation of the photoelectric effect.
In his first paper on the subject, Einstein did not yet write the formula E = mc² in the form that is famous today.
At CERN near Geneva, scientists observe every day how new particles with mass are created from energy.

teile.einleitung: Magnification tells you how much bigger or smaller an image is compared with the real object. You calculate it by dividing the image size by the object size. It plays an important role in photography, microscopy and projection.
wichtigste: Magnification is the image size divided by the object size.
It is also equal to the image distance divided by the object distance.
If it is greater than 1, the image is bigger than the object.
If it is less than 1, the image is reduced, as in a camera.
By the usual sign convention, a negative magnification means that the image is upside down.
A slide 24 mm high is projected to a height of 1.2 m with a magnification of 50.
With a magnification of 1 : 1 the image is exactly the same size as the object.

abschnitte.text: **Magnification** is often abbreviated with the Greek letter beta. It gives the ratio of the **image size** B to the **object size** G. The formula is: magnification equals B divided by G. A value of 2 means that the image is twice as big as the object. A value of 0.5 means that the image is half as big.

With a lens you can also calculate the magnification from the distances. It is equal to the **image distance** b, the distance from the image to the lens, divided by the **object distance** g. If an object is 30 cm in front of a lens and the image forms 15 cm behind it, the magnification is 15 divided by 30, that is 0.5. Together with the lens equation, you can then predict the size of the image. For example, an object 2 cm high placed 12 cm in front of a converging lens with a focal length of 8 cm gives an image 4 cm high.

In a **camera** large things are reduced onto a small sensor, so the magnification is much less than 1. If a house front 3 m high is to fill a sensor exactly 24 mm high, you need a scale of 1 : 125. A camera with a 50 mm focal length shows a person 1.8 m tall standing 10 m away only about 9 mm high. In **macro photography** you photograph small things such as insects at a scale of 1 : 1 or even larger. Then a fly is as big on the sensor as in real life.

With a **projector** it is the other way round: a small image is thrown onto a screen greatly enlarged. A slide 24 mm high is enlarged to a height of 1.2 m with a magnification of 50. The images in a **microscope** and a magnifying glass are also enlarged. For a microscope the magnification is usually given as, for example, 40 times or 400 times. The closer the object moves to the focal point of a converging lens, the bigger the image becomes.

A converging lens produces an **inverted image** on a screen, which is upside down. By the usual sign convention the magnification is then negative. A positive value means an upright image, like the one you see with a magnifying glass. In our eye, too, the image on the retina is upside down, and the brain turns it round. Often, though, people simply calculate with the absolute value, that is without the sign.

begriffe.erklaerung: The distance between the lens and the image.
The distance between the object and the lens.
The distance between the lens and the point at which parallel light rays meet.
Photographing very small things at life size or larger.

gewusst: If an object is exactly twice the focal length in front of a converging lens, the image is exactly the same size as the object.
The scale on a map, such as 1 : 25,000, follows the same idea as magnification.
In a pinhole camera the magnification depends only on the distances, without any lens at all.

teile.einleitung: Alpha radiation is a form of radioactive radiation in which an atomic nucleus flings out small particles. These alpha particles consist of two protons and two neutrons. In air they only travel a few centimetres, but inside the body they can do great damage.
wichtigste: An alpha particle consists of two protons and two neutrons, so it is a helium nucleus.
Alpha particles have a double positive charge.
In alpha decay the atomic number falls by 2 and the mass number by 4.
In air alpha radiation only travels a few centimetres.
Even a sheet of paper or the skin stops alpha radiation.
Breathed in or swallowed, alpha emitters are especially dangerous.
In a cloud chamber alpha particles show up as short, thick trails of mist.

abschnitte.text: Some atomic nuclei are unstable and break down by themselves; they are called **radioactive**. In alpha decay such a nucleus flings out an **alpha particle**. It consists of two protons and two neutrons and is therefore a helium nucleus. Because it contains two protons, it has a double positive charge. Alpha particles leave the nucleus at a few per cent of the speed of light.

When a nucleus gives off an alpha particle, it loses two protons and two neutrons. Its **atomic number** therefore falls by 2, and it becomes a different element. The **mass number** falls by 4. Uranium-238, for example, turns into thorium with the mass number 234.

Alpha particles are large and heavy and keep colliding with air particles. That is why they only travel a few centimetres in air. Even a sheet of paper or the outermost layer of skin stops them. From outside, alpha radiation is therefore hardly dangerous. It is quite different if an **alpha emitter** is breathed in or swallowed: then it releases all its energy into body cells in a tiny space and can badly damage them.

In 1899 the physicist **Ernest Rutherford** distinguished two kinds of radiation and named them after the Greek letters alpha and beta. Later he fired alpha particles at a thin gold foil and in this way discovered the tiny atomic nucleus in 1911. Alpha particles can be made visible in a **cloud chamber**. There they leave short, thick trails of mist, rather like the vapour trails of aeroplanes.

The artificial element **americium** is an alpha emitter and was often used in smoke detectors. There it makes the air in a small chamber conduct electricity; smoke disturbs this current and sets off the alarm. A natural alpha emitter is the noble gas **radon**, which can get into houses from the ground. In Switzerland radon occurs mainly in the Alps and the Jura, so the Federal Office of Public Health gives tips on airing rooms and sealing buildings.

begriffe.erklaerung: A helium nucleus made of two protons and two neutrons.
The property of some atomic nuclei to break down by themselves and give off radiation.
The number of protons in the nucleus; it determines the chemical element.
A device in which the paths of radiation particles become visible as trails of mist.

gewusst: A large part of the helium on Earth comes from alpha particles produced in rocks.
Alpha radiation is stopped by a single sheet of paper.
Space probes such as Voyager get their electricity from the heat of an alpha emitter, plutonium.

teile.einleitung: The sunset glow is the red, orange or pink light in the sky when the sun goes down. It happens because in the evening sunlight travels a particularly long way through the air. In the Alps even the mountain peaks turn red; this is called alpenglow.
wichtigste: The sunset glow happens because at sunset sunlight has a long way to travel through the air.
Blue light is scattered more strongly by the air than red light.
You see the sunset glow in the west, where the sun sets.
The setting sun often looks orange-red.
At midday the sun is not red, because its light has only a short way to go through the air.
Dust in the air can make a sunset glow especially strong.
The red glow of mountain peaks at sunset is called alpenglow.

abschnitte.text: The **sunset glow** is the reddish colouring of the sky and clouds during and shortly after sunset. Because the sun sets in the west, you see the sunset glow mainly in that direction. The matching glow in the east in the morning is called the **dawn glow**. Both are among the most beautiful light displays in the sky.

Sunlight looks white, but it is made of all the colours of the rainbow. When it passes through the air, blue light is bent off in all directions by the tiny air particles much more strongly than red light; this is called **Rayleigh scattering**. That is why the sky is blue during the day. In the evening the sun is low, and its light has to travel a very long way through the atmosphere before it reaches us.

On this long journey the blue light is almost completely scattered to the side. What is left are mainly the yellow, orange and **red parts** of the light. That is why the sun looks orange-red as it sets and colours the clouds to match. At midday the sun is high, its light has only a short way to go through the air, and so it looks yellowish white.

Dust, smoke and tiny droplets in the air can strengthen the sunset glow. After big **volcanic eruptions** such as that of Krakatoa in 1883, there were strikingly colourful sunsets all over the world for months. Saharan dust, which is sometimes blown as far as Switzerland, also produces intense colours. When clouds are lit from below, they often glow a particularly lovely pink or purple.

In the Alps the snow-covered peaks often glow red at sunset while the valleys already lie in shadow. This **alpenglow** is a popular subject for photos, for example on the Matterhorn, the Jungfrau or the Säntis. An old German weather saying goes: “Red sky in the evening brings fine weather.” It is often true, because a sunset glow shows that the sky is clear in the west, and in central Europe the weather usually comes from the west.

On Mars it is exactly the other way round: there the sky is reddish during the day, and at sunset a bluish glow appears around the sun. This is because of the fine dust in the thin Martian air, which scatters light differently from the Earth’s air. Photos of this have been taken, for example, by the Mars rover Curiosity. So a sunset on Mars is **bluish**.

begriffe.erklaerung: The bending of light in different directions by tiny particles.
The scattering of light by air particles, which affects blue light much more strongly than red.
The red glow of mountain peaks shortly after sunset.
The reddish colouring of the sky at sunrise.

gewusst: You can sometimes still see a sunset glow after the sun has already set for you, because clouds high up are still lit.
On Mars sunsets are blue; on Earth they are red.
After the eruption of Krakatoa in 1883 the evening sky over New York glowed so red that the fire brigade turned out because of a supposed fire.

t1ie9ito.t: Derivative of position with respect to time

teile.einleitung: How fast is a bike going at exactly this moment? The answer is given by the derivative of position with respect to time. It links the physics of motion with mathematics and is one of the most important tools of mechanics.
wichtigste: The derivative of position with respect to time gives the instantaneous velocity.
The second derivative of position with respect to time is the acceleration.
The derivative of acceleration with respect to time is called jerk.
In a position-time graph the instantaneous velocity is the gradient of the tangent.
The gradient of the secant between two points gives the average velocity.
Isaac Newton and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz developed differential calculus in the 17th century.
If the derivative is zero, the body is standing still at that moment.

abschnitte.text: A moving body is at a particular position x at every time t. This relationship is written as a function **x(t)** and drawn in a **position-time graph**. A straight line means steady motion. A curved line shows that the body is getting faster or slower.

If you join two points on the graph with a straight line, you get a **secant**. Its gradient is the average velocity between the two moments. If you move the two points closer and closer together, the secant becomes a **tangent**. Its gradient is the instantaneous velocity at exactly that moment. This is precisely what the derivative calculates; it is written v(t) = x'(t).

If a body moves according to x(t) = 3t² + 2t, its velocity is v(t) = 6t + 2. After 2 seconds it is therefore 14 m/s. For x(t) = 2t³ − 3t² you get v(t) = 6t² − 6t, so 36 m/s after 3 seconds. A ball with x(t) = −2t² + 8t has v(t) = −4t + 8; it stands still for a moment after 2 seconds. Oscillations can also be calculated this way: from x(t) = 4·sin(2t) it follows that v(t) = 8·cos(2t), so 8 m/s at time zero.

If you differentiate the velocity once more, you get the **acceleration**. It is therefore the second derivative of position. For x(t) = 5t³ you get a(t) = 30t, so 30 m/s² after one second. The next derivative is called **jerk**. A large jerk is unpleasant, so engineers design roller coasters, lifts and railway curves so that the jerk stays small.

The mathematics of derivatives is called **differential calculus**. Isaac Newton in England and Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz in Germany developed it independently of each other in the late 17th century. Newton needed it to describe the motion of the planets. The notation dx/dt comes from Leibniz and is still used today. The Bernoulli family of mathematicians from Basel and Leonhard Euler also greatly extended the method.

begriffe.erklaerung: The velocity at exactly one particular moment, as shown on a speedometer.
A mathematical tool that tells you how fast a quantity is changing at that moment.
A straight line that just touches a curve at one point.
A straight line that cuts a curve at two points.
How fast the acceleration changes.

gewusst: A car’s speedometer is really showing the derivative of position with respect to time all the time.
The derivatives after jerk even have joking English names: snap, crackle and pop.
Leonhard Euler from Basel wrote one of the first great textbooks of differential calculus.

teile.einleitung: The run-up is the fast running or riding before a jump or throw. During it the athlete builds up speed, that is kinetic energy. This energy is used at take-off or release to get further or higher.
wichtigste: During the run-up you build up speed and therefore kinetic energy.
In the long jump: the faster the run-up, the longer the jump.
Long jumpers measure out their run-up so that they hit the take-off exactly.
In the pole vault you run up with a long pole, in the javelin with the javelin in your hand.
In the modern high jump you run up in a curve.
Ski jumpers get their speed by going down the in-run.
Shot putters do not take a long run-up, because they have to stay in the circle.

abschnitte.text: A **run-up** is a stretch on which you build up momentum before a movement. In terms of physics, you build up **kinetic energy**. At take-off or release this energy is turned into height or distance. That is why you get much further with a run-up than from standing. You can easily try this out by jumping once from standing and once with a run-up.

In the **long jump**: the faster the run-up, the longer the jump. The best long jumpers are almost as fast as sprinters at take-off. So that they hit the **take-off board** exactly, they measure out their run-up in steps and put down a marker. If you step over the board, the jump does not count. In the triple jump, too, a fast, accurate run-up is decisive.

In the modern **high jump** you run up in a curve and jump over the bar backwards. This technique is called the Fosbury flop, after the American Dick Fosbury, who became Olympic champion with it in 1968. In the **pole vault** you run up with a long, flexible pole. The pole stores the energy of the run-up, bends and catapults the vaulter upwards.

In the **javelin** you run up with the javelin in your hand and then throw it from behind a line. The run-up gives the javelin extra momentum. Shot putters, on the other hand, do not take a long run-up, because they have to stay in the throwing circle. They build up their momentum with a spin or a glide inside the circle.

Ski jumpers get their speed by going down the **in-run**. On big hills they reach almost 100 km/h this way. The Swiss ski jumper Simon Ammann won Olympic gold in ski jumping four times. In gymnastics you take a run-up to the **vaulting table**, jump onto a springboard and push off with your hands. Here, too, a fast, controlled run-up decides the height of the vault.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy that a body has because of its speed.
The board in the long jump from which you have to take off.
A high jump technique in which you jump over the bar backwards.
The steep track down which ski jumpers travel to the take-off.

gewusst: From standing, even good athletes only jump a little over three metres; with a run-up, over eight metres.
Many ski jumps today have an in-run made of ice so that the skis glide quickly and evenly.
Thanks to the run-up and the pole, pole vaulters get over six metres high.

teile.einleitung: A roller coaster is a ride in a theme park on which cars race over steep hills, through bends and sometimes through loops. The exciting thing about it is pure physics: after the first hill the train usually carries on without any motor at all. The energy it needs is stored in the height.
wichtigste: On a classic roller coaster a chain lift pulls the train up the first hill.
The first hill is usually the highest, because no more energy is added after that.
Going downhill, potential energy is turned into kinetic energy.
The roller coaster is fastest at the lowest point.
Without friction the mass of the passengers has no effect on the speed.
Launched roller coasters are strongly accelerated by motors at the start.
Many modern roller coasters brake with eddy current brakes without touching the rails.

abschnitte.text: A roller coaster consists of rails on which a train of several cars runs. The German name means “figure-of-eight ride” and comes from early rides whose track ran in the shape of an eight. There are **wooden roller coasters** and **steel roller coasters**, with steel allowing tight bends and loops. Ice slides, which people rode down in Russia as early as the 17th century, are regarded as their forerunners. That is why in some languages roller coasters are still called “Russian mountains” today.

First a **chain lift** slowly pulls the train up to the highest point. There the train has a lot of **potential energy**. As it rolls down, this energy is turned into **kinetic energy**, and it gets faster and faster. When it climbs again, it slows down, because the kinetic energy turns back into potential energy. Because some energy is lost through friction, every further hill must be lower than the first.

Without friction you can calculate the speed at the bottom with the formula v equals the square root of 2 times g times h. With a drop of 45 metres and g equal to 10 m/s², this gives 30 m/s, that is 108 km/h. Mass does not appear in this formula, so a full train is as fast as an empty one. This is because a heavy train has more potential energy, but also has more mass to accelerate. In reality the air and rolling friction slow it down a little.

On a **launched roller coaster** motors accelerate the train to a high speed within a few seconds at the start. This is often done with linear motors that work with magnetic fields. In a **loop** the centrifugal force presses the passengers into their seats, so that they do not fall out even upside down. Modern loops are not perfectly round but tighter at the top, so that the forces stay more comfortable for the body.

At the end of the ride the train must stop safely. Many modern rides use **eddy current brakes**. Metal fins on the train pass between strong magnets, and the magnetic fields brake without any contact. These brakes hardly wear out and even work without electricity. In addition, lap bars and belts hold the passengers securely in their seats.

Many Swiss families visit Europa-Park in Rust in Germany, which is not far from Basel. There are many big roller coasters there. In Switzerland, too, there are smaller theme parks with roller coasters. Roller coasters are also put up at fairs such as the Basel Autumn Fair.

begriffe.erklaerung: Energy that a body has because it is high up.
Energy that a body has because it is moving.
A moving chain that pulls the train up the first hill.
A brake that slows things down with magnets without touching the rails.

gewusst: On some roller coasters passengers feel several times their body weight when they go through a bend at the bottom.
At the top of a hill you can feel almost weightless for a moment; this is called airtime.
Without friction a fully loaded train is just as fast as an empty one.

teile.einleitung: Albert Einstein was one of the most famous physicists of all time. With his theory of relativity he completely changed our picture of space, time and energy. He had his most important ideas in Switzerland, while he was working at the patent office in Bern.
wichtigste: Albert Einstein was born in 1879 in Ulm in Germany and died in 1955 in Princeton in the USA.
He studied at the Polytechnic in Zurich, today’s ETH.
In 1901 he became a Swiss citizen.
From 1902 he worked at the Federal Patent Office in Bern.
In his miracle year of 1905 he published several ground-breaking papers, including the formula E = mc².
He was awarded the Nobel Prize in Physics for the year 1921.
In 1933 he moved to the USA, where he lived until his death.

abschnitte.text: Albert Einstein was born on 14 March 1879 in **Ulm** and grew up in Munich. As a teenager he attended the cantonal school in **Aarau** and passed his school-leaving exam there. After that, from 1896 to 1900, he studied physics and mathematics at the **Polytechnic in Zurich**. In 1901 he became a Swiss citizen.

Because he could not find a job at a university, Einstein worked from 1902 at the **Federal Patent Office** in Bern. There he examined inventions and thought about physics in his spare time. For a while he lived at **Kramgasse 49** in Bern’s old town. He met friends for discussions and jokingly called the group the “Olympia Academy”.

In 1905 Einstein published several papers that changed physics. He explained that light consists of small packets of energy, and so provided the explanation for the **photoelectric effect**. He set out the **special theory of relativity**, according to which time and space are not the same for everyone. From this came the famous formula **E = mc²**: mass and energy can be turned into each other. In the same year he wrote his doctoral thesis at the University of Zurich.

In 1915, in Berlin, Einstein completed the **general theory of relativity**. It describes gravity as the curving of space and time by large masses. You can imagine it like a heavy ball on a stretched sheet, which makes a dip. In 1919 measurements during a solar eclipse confirmed that light is bent by the sun.

Einstein was awarded the **Nobel Prize in Physics** for the year 1921, for his explanation of the photoelectric effect. When the Nazis came to power in Germany in 1933, he was persecuted as a Jew. He moved to the USA and did research in **Princeton** until his death on 18 April 1955. All his life he campaigned for peace.

Without Einstein’s theories the **GPS** in your phone would calculate inaccurately, because clocks in satellites run differently from those on Earth. Lasers and solar cells are also based on his ideas about light. In Bern you can visit the **Einstein House** on the Kramgasse. The Bern Historical Museum also has a large exhibition about his life.

begriffe.erklaerung: Einstein’s theory that explains how space, time and gravity are connected.
A formula that says mass contains a huge amount of energy; c is the speed of light.
An authority that examines and protects new inventions.
Light can knock electrons out of a metal.

gewusst: The chemical element einsteinium is named after Albert Einstein.
Einstein was a citizen of Switzerland and kept his Swiss citizenship until the end of his life.
His most famous formula came about while he was still working during the day as an examiner at the patent office.

teile.einleitung: Attraction is a force that pulls things towards each other. You probably know it best from magnets that hold paper clips or nails. But not everything is attracted by a magnet, and that is exactly what makes experiments so exciting.
wichtigste: The force with which a magnet pulls iron towards it is called attraction.
Things that a magnet can attract are called magnetic.
Magnets mainly attract iron, nickel and cobalt.
Wood, gold, aluminium, glass and plastic are not attracted.
Both poles of a magnet attract an iron nail.
A magnet can attract from a short distance without touching.
The magnetic force also works through cardboard, paper and water.

abschnitte.text: In **attraction** two things move towards each other. A magnet attracts an iron nail even before it touches it. The closer the nail gets, the stronger the force becomes. Both poles of the magnet, the **north pole** and the **south pole**, attract iron. Between two magnets only unlike poles attract each other; like poles repel each other.

Objects that a magnet attracts are called **magnetic**. These include above all things made of iron and steel, but also of nickel and cobalt. A wooden ball, a ring of real gold or a drinks can made of aluminium are not attracted. The Swiss 5-centime coin also stays where it is, because it is made of a copper alloy. A tin can made of tinplate, which is thin steel, on the other hand, is attracted.

Put a **paper clip** on a thin piece of cardboard and move a magnet underneath it. The paper clip moves along with it, because the attraction works through the cardboard. This also works through a glass of water or through your hand. If you hang several paper clips one below the other on a magnet, they briefly become small magnets themselves. In this way you can make a whole chain.

It is not only magnets that attract. The Earth pulls all objects towards it; that is **gravity**. That is why an apple falls from a tree. Electric charges also attract each other when one is positive and one is negative. That is why a rubbed balloon attracts small scraps of paper or your hair.

Magnets hold drawings on the fridge and close bags and cupboard doors. At recycling centres large magnets separate iron and steel from other waste. The needle of a **compass** is a small magnet that the Earth’s magnetic field points to the north. More than 2000 years ago people in Greece and China already knew stones that attract iron. These stones made of magnetite gave the magnet its name.

begriffe.erklaerung: Attracted by a magnet, for example iron.
The places at the ends of a magnet where the force is strongest.
The invisible area round a magnet in which its force acts.
The attraction with which the Earth pulls all things towards it.

gewusst: Not every coin is magnetic, but some euro coins with a steel core are attracted by magnets.
The name magnet probably comes from the region of Magnesia in Greece, where magnetic stones were found.
The Earth itself is also a giant magnet; otherwise no compass would work.

teile.einleitung: Aerodynamics is the science of how air flows around moving bodies. It explains why aeroplanes fly, why racing cars have wings and why golf balls have dimples. In sport, good aerodynamics can decide between victory and defeat.
wichtigste: Aerodynamics studies how air flows around moving bodies.
Air resistance slows down everything that moves through the air.
In wind tunnels engineers and sports teams measure how strongly the air slows things down.
Aeroplane wings produce lift, while Formula One wings press the car down onto the road.
The dimples on a golf ball reduce air resistance.
Tight, smooth racing suits and pointed time-trial helmets let the air flow away better.
In places high up, the thinner air slows things down less.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from Greek: “aer” means air and “dynamis” means force. **Aerodynamics** is a branch of fluid dynamics. It studies the forces that arise when air flows past a body. The most important are the braking **air resistance**, also called drag, and **lift**, which acts at right angles to the flow.

An aeroplane wing is shaped and tilted slightly so that it deflects the air downwards. The air flows faster over the top, and the pressure above the wing is lower than below it. This pushes the wing upwards; that is lift. The German Otto Lilienthal studied this in the 1890s with his own gliding flights. In 1903 the Wright brothers made the first powered flight.

With cars the main aim is low air resistance, so that they use less energy. How streamlined a car is, is described by the **drag coefficient**, or Cd value for short. Formula One cars have large wings at the front and back that work like upside-down aeroplane wings. They press the car onto the road so that it does not skid in bends. This force is called **downforce**.

Cycling and ski teams measure the air resistance of their athletes in a **wind tunnel**. In time trials, cyclists wear helmets with a long, pointed shape so that the air flows away better. On the track a closed disc wheel is often used at the back to avoid air swirls from the spokes. Speed skaters and skiers wear very tight, smooth suits. And because the air is thinner at altitude, sprint and cycling records are often easier to achieve in places high up.

A golf ball has several hundred small dimples. They make a thin, swirling layer of air form right on the surface. As a result, the airflow only separates from the ball further back, and the **wake** of swirling air behind the ball becomes smaller. This lowers the air resistance, and the ball flies much further than a smooth ball.

Many ideas in aerodynamics come from nature. Birds have curved wings and spread their feathers at the wing tips to reduce swirls. Many aeroplanes today have similar upturned wing tips, known as **winglets**. The shape of dolphins and penguins also shows how to glide through a medium with little resistance.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force with which the air slows down a moving body.
The force that pushes a wing upwards.
A facility in which air is blown in a controlled way past models or people.
A number that shows how streamlined a shape is.

gewusst: A golf ball without dimples would only fly about half as far.
At high speed a cyclist has to use most of their effort against air resistance.
The Swiss Formula One team Sauber in Hinwil has its own wind tunnel.

teile.einleitung: The alphorn is a long wooden wind instrument known above all from Switzerland. It has no finger holes and no keys, yet you can play whole tunes on it. Its warm, far-carrying sound can be heard across valleys and mountainsides.
wichtigste: The alphorn is usually made of wood, often spruce.
It is especially well known from Switzerland and is regarded as a typical Swiss instrument.
An alphorn has no finger holes and no keys.
The player makes the different notes with the lips alone.
In the past herders used the alphorn to give signals.
The end of the alphorn curves upwards and is called the bell.
Because of its loud, far-carrying sound, it can be heard a very long way.

abschnitte.text: An alphorn is usually about 3 to 4 metres long and consists of a long, conical **wooden tube**. Conical means that the tube gets wider and wider from the mouthpiece to the end. At the end it curves upwards and opens into the **bell**. In the past people looked for spruce trees that had grown on steep slopes and had become curved at the bottom by themselves. Today the parts are hollowed out and glued together by instrument makers, and often wrapped with rattan cane.

The player presses their lips against a mouthpiece and makes them **vibrate** while blowing in. This sets the column of air in the tube vibrating, and **sound waves** are produced. The longer the tube, the lower the fundamental note. In terms of physics, an alphorn is therefore similar to a trumpet, only much longer and without valves.

Because there are no finger holes, an alphorn can only play certain notes, the **natural notes**. The player chooses them by tightening or loosening the lips and giving more or less air. Higher natural notes lie close together, so tunes are usually played in the upper range. One special note lies between F and F sharp and is often called the **alphorn fa**. It sounds a little unusual to our ears and gives the music its typical character.

Herders in the Alps used to use the alphorn to give **signals**, for example to call the cows or to communicate with other alpine pastures. In the evening they also played a prayer or a tune on it to calm the animals. Over time the instrument was almost forgotten. In the 19th century it became popular again with alpine herders’ festivals, and since then it has been regarded as a **symbol of Switzerland**.

Today you hear the alphorn at yodelling festivals, at celebrations on 1 August and at tourist events in the mountains. Many alphorn players play in groups, often in threes or fours. There is also modern music, jazz and orchestral pieces for alphorn. For travelling there are alphorns that can be taken apart into three pieces.

begriffe.erklaerung: A note that a tube without holes or keys can produce by itself.
The air inside the tube, which vibrates when the instrument is played.
The wide, upturned end of the alphorn, where the sound comes out.
The small part at the start of the tube against which you put your lips.

gewusst: The composer Johannes Brahms used an alphorn tune he had heard in Switzerland in his first symphony.
In calm weather an alphorn can be heard several kilometres away in the mountains.
Many alphorns are so long that the bell rests on the ground while they are played.

teile.einleitung: In physics, work means something very specific: a force moves a body over a distance. Anyone who pushes a box or carries a rucksack up the stairs is doing work. Anyone who just holds a bag still, on the other hand, is doing no work in the physical sense, even if their arms get tired.
wichtigste: Mechanical work is force times distance, when both point in the same direction.
The unit of work is the joule.
One joule equals one newton metre.
Without movement in the direction of the force, no work is done.
Work is energy that has been transferred.
The unit joule is named after the English physicist James Prescott Joule.
Work per unit of time is called power, measured in watts.

abschnitte.text: Physical **work** is done when a force moves a body along a path. The formula is W = F · s, that is **force times distance**. Force and distance must point in the same direction. If you hold a heavy bag still in the air, it does not move, and you do no work on it. Your muscles still get tired, though, because they are constantly working on the inside.

If you push a trolley with 50 N over 20 m, you do 50 · 20 = 1000 J of work. If a bike pulls a trailer with 40 N over 2 km, that is 80,000 J or 80 kJ. A crane that lifts a load of 2.5 kN by 0.4 m also does 1000 J. You can also rearrange the formula: 1500 J over 300 m means a force of 5 N. And 400 J with 8 N means that the force acted over 50 m.

The unit of work is the **joule**, abbreviated J. One joule is the work done when a force of one newton acts over one metre, that is one **newton metre**. If you lift a 100 g bar of chocolate by one metre, you do roughly one joule of work. Work is closely related to **energy**: anyone who does work transfers energy to a body. If a stone is lifted up, it stores this energy as potential energy.

When lifting, you do **lifting work**, which is weight times height. When accelerating, it is called acceleration work, and when pushing across the ground, work against friction. With a ramp or a pulley you need less force, but a longer distance. The work stays the same; this is called the **golden rule of mechanics**.

The term work in physics was introduced around 1829 by the French engineer Gaspard-Gustave de Coriolis. In the 1840s the English brewer and physicist **James Prescott Joule** showed that work can be turned into heat. He made a paddle wheel turn in water and measured how the water got warmer. The unit joule is named after him.

begriffe.erklaerung: Force times distance, that is the energy transferred when a body is moved.
The unit of work and energy.
The work you do when lifting a body up.
How much work is done per second, measured in watts.

gewusst: If you weigh 40 kg and climb stairs 3 m high, you do around 1200 J of lifting work.
Food packaging shows the energy content in kilojoules, the same unit as work.
One kilowatt hour of electricity corresponds to 3.6 million joules.

teile.einleitung: Optical aberrations are faults that stop a lens or mirror from producing an image that is completely sharp or completely true to shape. Instead of a fine point a small blur appears, lines become curved or edges get coloured fringes. Opticians fight these faults with cleverly combined lenses.
wichtigste: Optical aberrations make the images of lenses and mirrors worse.
Ludwig von Seidel distinguished five monochromatic aberrations.
In spherical aberration the edge rays of a converging lens are bent more strongly than rays near the axis.
Stopping down, that is using a smaller aperture, reduces spherical aberration.
Aspherical lenses largely avoid spherical aberration.
In distortion, straight lines at the edge of the image appear curved.
Coma makes a point look like a comet with a tail when light comes in at an angle.

abschnitte.text: An ideal lens would form each point of an object again as a sharp point. Real lenses with spherically ground surfaces never quite manage this. The deviations are called **optical aberrations**. A distinction is made between faults that occur even with light of a single colour and faults caused by the different colours of light. In 1856 the mathematician **Ludwig von Seidel** described the five most important faults for single-coloured, that is monochromatic, light.

In **spherical aberration** the outer zones of a converging lens bend light more strongly than the centre.
