As a result the edge rays meet at a different point from the rays near the axis, and the image becomes a little blurred. A simple remedy is **stopping down**: a smaller aperture only lets through the rays near the centre. Better still are **aspherical lenses**, whose surfaces are not ground to an exact sphere. Today they are found in many cameras and mobile phone lenses.

When light enters a lens at an angle, **coma** occurs, in which a point looks like a comet with a tail. In **astigmatism**, slanting beams of light are not focused to a point but to two separate lines at different distances. In **field curvature** the sharp image does not lie on a flat plane but on a curved surface. Then the centre and edge of the image cannot both be sharp at the same time on a flat sensor. Together with spherical aberration and distortion, these are the five Seidel aberrations.

With **distortion** the image is sharp, but warped. Straight lines at the edge of the image appear curved. If they bend outwards, it is called barrel distortion; if they bend inwards, pincushion distortion. Distortion is especially strong in **fisheye lenses**, which deliberately show a very wide angle of view. Today many cameras and mobile phones correct this fault automatically with software.

Glass bends blue light more strongly than red, so simple lenses have a slightly different focal point for each colour. This **colour fault**, chromatic aberration, produces coloured fringes along bright edges. If you combine two lenses made of different types of glass, you get an **achromat**, which greatly reduces this fault. Good camera lenses therefore consist of many individual lenses that correct each other. The Hubble Space Telescope also had an optical fault after its launch in 1990, which was corrected during a repair mission in space in 1993.

begriffe.erklaerung: Another word for an optical fault in an image.
A lens that is thicker in the middle and gathers light rays at one point.
An adjustable opening that determines how much light passes through a camera lens.
A combination of lenses that greatly reduces colour faults.
A fault in which straight lines in the image appear curved.

gewusst: The mirror of the Hubble telescope was ground wrongly at the edge by only about two thousandths of a millimetre.
The human eye also has optical aberrations, and the brain makes up for many of them.
A modern camera lens can consist of more than ten individual lenses.

teile.einleitung: An absorption spectrum shows which colours or wavelengths of light a substance swallows. If you send white light through a gas, certain colours are missing afterwards and show up as dark lines. These lines are like a fingerprint that lets you recognise substances even on distant stars.
wichtigste: An absorption spectrum forms when light with a continuous spectrum passes through a cooler gas.
The gas swallows very particular wavelengths, which are then missing as dark lines.
According to Kirchhoff’s law of radiation, a gas absorbs exactly the wavelengths that it also gives out.
Every chemical element has its own pattern of lines.
Chlorophyll in plants absorbs mainly blue and red light.
Carbon dioxide and water vapour absorb strongly in the infrared and so contribute to the greenhouse effect.
The ozone in the stratosphere absorbs a large part of the sun’s UV radiation.

abschnitte.text: White light contains all colours, as you can see in a rainbow or behind a prism. Such a band of colours without gaps is called a **continuous spectrum**. If this light passes through a cooler gas, the gas swallows individual colours. Dark lines then appear in the spectrum, and the result is called an **absorption spectrum**.

The electrons in an atom can only take on very particular energy levels. If light with exactly the right energy hits the atom, it lifts an electron to a higher level and is swallowed in the process. Light with a different energy simply carries on. That is why only very particular wavelengths are missing. According to **Kirchhoff’s law of radiation**, they are the same wavelengths that a hot gas of the same substance gives out as bright lines.

Around 1814 the German optician Joseph von Fraunhofer discovered hundreds of dark lines in the light of the sun. Today they are called **Fraunhofer lines**. Around 1860 Gustav Kirchhoff and Robert Bunsen explained that these lines come from gases in the sun’s atmosphere. This made it possible to find out what substances the sun is made of without ever having been there. The element helium was even discovered first in the solar spectrum and only found on Earth later.

The colours of things are also linked to absorption. A pane of glass with red dye absorbs the other colours and lets mainly red through, which is why it looks red. Leaves look green because **chlorophyll** swallows blue and red light for photosynthesis and reflects green. In chemistry a **photometer** is used to measure how much light a solution swallows.

How strongly a substance swallows light is described by its **absorbance**. With an absorbance of 1, 10 per cent of the light still gets through; with an absorbance of 2, only 1 per cent. According to the **Beer-Lambert law**, absorbance equals the absorption coefficient times concentration times path length. If a solution in a 1 cm cuvette has an absorbance of 0.6 and a coefficient of 12,000 L/(mol · cm), the concentration is 0.00005 mol/L.

The Earth’s atmosphere acts like a huge filter. The **ozone** in the stratosphere absorbs a large part of the dangerous UV radiation and so protects skin and eyes. Carbon dioxide and water vapour, on the other hand, absorb heat radiation in the **infrared**. As a result heat stays in the atmosphere, which is called the greenhouse effect. Today researchers also use absorption spectra to measure how much greenhouse gas is in the air.

begriffe.erklaerung: The splitting of light into its individual colours or wavelengths.
The distance between two wave crests; it determines the colour of light.
The swallowing of light by a substance.
A number that shows how strongly a sample weakens light.
A narrow bright or dark line at a particular wavelength in the spectrum.

gewusst: The element helium was first discovered in the light of the sun in 1868, before it was found on Earth.
With absorption spectra researchers can even study the air of planets around distant stars.
Without the absorption of UV light by ozone, life on land would hardly be possible.

teile.einleitung: The principle of action is the second of Newton’s three laws of mechanics. It says how strongly a body accelerates when a force acts on it. Its short formula F = m · a is one of the most famous equations in physics.
wichtigste: The basic equation of the second law is F equals m times a.
The greater the force, the greater the acceleration.
If you triple the force, the acceleration also triples.
If the same force acts on twice the mass, the acceleration halves.
The unit of force is the newton; 1 N corresponds to 1 kg · m/s².
Isaac Newton published the law in 1687 in his work “Principia”.
For acceleration it is always the resultant force that counts, that is the sum of all forces.

abschnitte.text: The **principle of action** is also called Newton’s second law or the fundamental law of mechanics. It links three quantities: the **force** F, the **mass** m and the **acceleration** a. The formula F = m · a means: a force changes the speed of a body. A heavy body needs more force than a light one for the same acceleration.

To accelerate 2 kg at 3 m/s², you need 2 · 3 = 6 N. If a force of 12 N acts on a trolley of 4 kg, it accelerates at 12 : 4 = 3 m/s². A car of 1000 kg needs a force of 2000 N for 2 m/s². If a force of 600 N accelerates a body at 4 m/s², it has a mass of 150 kg. So you can rearrange the formula for any of the three quantities.

A bike and its rider together weigh 80 kg. If, after subtracting air resistance and friction, a **resultant force** of 40 N remains, they accelerate at 0.5 m/s². A football of 0.5 kg that is accelerated at 20 m/s² when kicked experiences a force of 10 N. An empty shopping trolley is easy to push off, a full one only with effort. That is exactly what the principle of action describes.

The English physicist **Isaac Newton** presented the law in 1687 in his book “Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica”. In it he described three laws: the principle of inertia, the principle of action and the principle of interaction. Newton actually formulated it in terms of **momentum**: force equals the change in momentum per unit of time. The unit newton was later named after him.

With the principle of action experts calculate how strong brakes, engines and rocket motors need to be. The orbits of planets and satellites can also be worked out with it. Weight is a special case: F = m · g with g ≈ 9.81 m/s² on Earth. Only at very high speeds close to the speed of light do you need Albert Einstein’s more precise theory of relativity.

begriffe.erklaerung: Something that can accelerate or deform a body, measured in newtons.
How much matter a body has and how sluggish it is, measured in kilograms.
How fast the speed changes, measured in m/s².
The force that is left when you add all the forces together.

gewusst: One newton is roughly the weight of a 100 g bar of chocolate.
Rockets keep getting lighter in flight because they burn fuel, and so with the same thrust they accelerate more and more strongly.
Newton wrote his “Principia” in Latin, the language of science at that time.

teile.einleitung: An accumulator, usually just called a rechargeable battery, is a battery that you can charge again and again. It stores electrical energy and gives it out again later. Without rechargeable batteries there would be no mobile phones, tablets or e-bikes.
wichtigste: A rechargeable battery is a store for electrical energy that can be recharged.
Almost every mobile phone has a rechargeable battery built in.
When the battery is flat, you charge it up again with a charger.
The battery symbol on a phone shows how full the battery is.
After many years of use a rechargeable battery does not last as long.
Heat, for example in a car in the sun, damages a rechargeable battery.
Old rechargeable batteries do not belong in the rubbish, but back in the shop at the collection point.

abschnitte.text: A normal battery is finished when its energy has been used up. An **accumulator**, on the other hand, can be recharged hundreds of times. The word comes from Latin and means something like collector or store. In everyday German people often just say “Akku”, and sometimes simply battery.

Inside a rechargeable battery there are two terminals, the **positive terminal** and the **negative terminal**, separated by a conducting liquid or paste. When it discharges, chemical reactions take place that make electrons flow through the connected device. When it charges, the charger pushes current in the opposite direction. This reverses the chemical reactions, and the battery is full again.

Mobile phones, tablets, laptops and wireless headphones almost always have a **lithium-ion battery**. On an e-bike, too, a rechargeable battery gives the motor its energy. Electric cars contain very large batteries with thousands of individual cells. Normal cars with a petrol engine have a **lead-acid battery** that supplies the starter motor with electricity.

In 1859 the French physicist **Gaston Planté** built the first usable lead-acid battery. Later came nickel-cadmium and nickel-metal hydride batteries. In 1991 the company Sony brought the first lithium-ion battery onto the market. Three researchers received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 2019 for developing it.

Rechargeable batteries age over time and after a few years do not last as long. Heat is especially bad for them, so you should never leave a phone in a hot car in the sun. Great cold also weakens a battery for a while. Many experts recommend not letting lithium-ion batteries run completely flat all the time. A damaged or swollen battery can become dangerous and should be handled by experts.

Rechargeable batteries contain substances that harm the environment, so they do not belong in the normal rubbish. In Switzerland you take old rechargeable and ordinary batteries back to the shop, to the **collection point**. Shops that sell batteries must also take them back. When you buy them, you pay a small **advance recycling fee**, which pays for the recycling. Valuable metals are recovered from old batteries.

begriffe.erklaerung: An energy store that can be recharged again and again.
Charging fully once and then discharging again.
The most common type of rechargeable battery today in phones, laptops and electric cars.
Processing old things so that the raw materials can be used again.

gewusst: The first lead-acid battery of 1859 works in principle in the same way as the battery in today’s petrol cars.
An electric car battery can store as much energy as hundreds of phone batteries together.
Many small devices such as toothbrushes or toys also contain a rechargeable battery that should be recycled.

teile.einleitung: The anti-lock braking system, ABS for short, is a technology in cars and motorbikes that stops the wheels from locking during an emergency stop. This keeps the vehicle steerable, so you can still swerve round an obstacle. Today ABS is fitted in almost all new cars.
wichtigste: ABS stops the wheels from locking during an emergency stop.
Rolling wheels can still be steered; locked wheels only skid straight ahead.
Sensors constantly measure the speed of each wheel.
When the ABS is working, you often feel a juddering or pulsing in the brake pedal.
Electronic ABS first came onto the market in production cars in the 1970s.
The anti-skid system ESP uses the sensors of the ABS.
On loose gravel or fresh snow the braking distance can be longer with ABS than without.

abschnitte.text: If you brake very hard without ABS, the wheels can stop turning. They **lock** and skid over the road. A skidding wheel can no longer be steered, and the car simply carries on straight ahead. The **anti-lock braking system** prevents this by briefly reducing the braking force at the right moment.

At each wheel a **wheel speed sensor** measures how fast it is turning. A control unit compares the values many times a second. If it notices that a wheel is suddenly slowing down sharply and about to lock, it briefly lowers the brake pressure at that wheel. As soon as the wheel is rolling again, the pressure is increased again. You feel this rapid releasing and braking as a juddering or **pulsing** in the brake pedal.

**Friction** acts between the tyre and the road. As long as the wheel is rolling, static friction acts, which is stronger and makes steering possible. If the wheel skids, only the weaker **sliding friction** acts. That is why a rolling wheel usually brakes better on a dry road and can still be steered at the same time. On loose gravel or fresh snow, however, a locked wheel pushes a braking wedge of material in front of it, so there the braking distance can be longer with ABS.

The first anti-lock systems already existed earlier in aeroplanes and trains. Electronic ABS for cars went into series production in the 1970s, in 1978 in the Mercedes-Benz S-Class with technology from Bosch. In the following decades ABS became cheaper and more widespread. Today it is standard on new cars in Europe.

On a motorbike ABS is especially helpful, because a locked front wheel easily leads to a fall. Further assistance systems build on ABS. **ESP**, the electronic stability programme, uses the ABS sensors and prevents skidding in bends. To do so it brakes individual wheels in a targeted way. Even so, no system replaces a sensible speed and enough distance.

begriffe.erklaerung: When a wheel stops turning while braking and skids over the road.
The friction as long as two surfaces are not sliding against each other.
The weaker friction when two surfaces slide along each other.
A driver assistance system that stops a car from skidding.

gewusst: With ABS you can press the brake fully in an emergency stop and steer at the same time.
ABS adjusts the brake pressure many times a second.
Modern bikes and e-bikes are now also available with ABS.

teile.einleitung: The launch angle is the angle relative to the ground at which a ball, a javelin or a shot is thrown. Together with the speed, it decides how high and how far something flies. If you know the right angle, you can throw and jump further in sport.
wichtigste: The launch angle is measured between the direction of flight at release and the horizontal ground.
Without air resistance a ball flies furthest if you throw it at 45 degrees.
Two angles that add up to 90 degrees, for example 30 and 60 degrees, give the same distance without air resistance.
Twice the launch speed gives four times the distance.
At 90 degrees the ball flies straight up and lands back where it was thrown from.
Good long jumpers take off at only about 20 degrees.
Shot putters push the shot a little flatter than 45 degrees, because it leaves the hand above the ground.

abschnitte.text: If you throw an object upwards at a slant, it follows a curved path. This path is called a **trajectory parabola**, because it has the shape of a parabola. The **launch angle** is the angle between the starting direction and the horizontal ground. At 0 degrees you throw flat, at 90 degrees straight up.

In a slanted throw the motion can be split into two parts. Horizontally the ball keeps flying steadily, while vertically **gravity** slows it down and pulls it back down. Without air resistance the distance is: v squared times sin(2α) divided by g. So at 10 m/s and 45 degrees, with g equal to 10 m/s², a ball flies 10 metres. Because the speed appears squared, throwing twice as fast gives four times the distance.

A flat throw moves forward quickly but lands early. A steep throw stays in the air for a long time but hardly moves forward. At **45 degrees** the best balance between flight time and forward speed is reached. Angles that are the same distance from 45 degrees, such as 30 and 60 degrees, give the same distance, but the steeper throw flies higher.

In real sport the best angle often looks different. Long jumpers take off at about **20 degrees**, because otherwise they would lose too much run-up speed. In the **shot put** the best angle is a little under 45 degrees, because the shot is released at a height of about two metres. The Swiss athlete Werner Günthör became world champion in the shot put in 1987, 1991 and 1993. In the javelin and discus, too, professionals throw much flatter than 45 degrees.

In reality the air slows down every thrown object. As a result the end of the trajectory becomes steeper and the distance shorter. With light balls such as a shuttlecock this **air resistance** is especially strong. That is why the best angle with air is usually less than 45 degrees.

begriffe.erklaerung: The curved flight path of an object thrown at a slant.
How fast an object is moving at the moment it is let go.
How strongly the Earth pulls things down, about 9.81 m/s², often rounded to 10.
The braking force of the air on everything that moves.

gewusst: Back in the 17th century Galileo Galilei found out that thrown objects fly along a parabola.
On the Moon a ball thrown the same way would fly about six times as far as on Earth.
Without air, a ball thrown at 30 degrees flies as far as one thrown at 60 degrees.

teile.einleitung: Twin research studies twins in order to find out what shapes us as humans. It asks: how much of our characteristics comes from our genes and how much from our environment? Because twins grow up at the same time, they are ideal pairs for comparison.
wichtigste: Identical twins have practically the same genetic material.
Non-identical twins share on average about half of their genetic material, like other siblings.
Researchers compare both kinds of twins to tell apart the influence of genes and environment.
Francis Galton in the 19th century is regarded as the founder of twin research.
Identical twins who grew up apart are especially revealing.
The share of differences that comes from genes is called heritability.
Even identical twins have different fingerprints.

abschnitte.text: **Twin research** is a branch of science that compares pairs of twins with each other. For example, it measures height, health, talents or personality traits. Then it looks at how similar the two are. From this you can estimate what role **genes** and what role the **environment** play. Environment means everything a person experiences: family, school, friends, food and much more.

**Identical twins** have practically the same genetic material and therefore usually look very alike. Their blood group is practically always the same. **Non-identical twins**, on the other hand, share on average only about half of their genetic material, just like other siblings. They can also be a boy and a girl. Even so, both kinds of twins grow up at the same time in the same family.

If a characteristic is much more similar in identical twins than in non-identical ones, that points to a strong influence of genes. If both kinds are about equally similar, the environment plays a bigger role. From such comparisons researchers calculate **heritability**. It shows what share of the differences between people in a group comes from genes. Heritability, however, says nothing about how strongly an individual person is determined by their genes.

The Englishman **Francis Galton** is regarded as the founder of twin research. He was a cousin of Charles Darwin and was already studying pairs of twins in the 1870s. From 1979 the famous **Minnesota Twin Study** took place in the USA. It examined identical twins who had grown up apart in different families. They have the same genes but a different environment, and are therefore especially valuable for research.

A well-known recent study was carried out by NASA with the identical twins Scott and Mark Kelly. Both were astronauts. Scott spent almost a year on the International Space Station, while Mark stayed on Earth. Afterwards experts compared their bodies closely to see how a long stay in space changes a human being. Most of the changes went back to normal after his return.

Twin research shows that almost all characteristics are influenced both by genes and by the environment. For height or eye colour, genes play a big role. For likes, hobbies or the language you speak, the environment is decisive. That is why even identical twins are never completely the same. Every person stays unique, even if there seem to be two of them.

begriffe.erklaerung: The building instructions for the body that are found in every cell.
A section of the genetic material that helps determine a particular characteristic.
Everything a person experiences and everything that affects them from outside.
How much of the differences in a characteristic within a group comes from genes.
A scientific investigation with many participants.

gewusst: Identical twins do not have the same fingerprints, because these depend on small chance events before birth.
In the Minnesota study some twins who had grown up apart met for the first time as adults.
Francis Galton made the English pair of words “nature and nurture” well known, meaning inborn qualities and environment.

teile.einleitung: Adaptive optics is a technique that lets large telescopes take sharp pictures even though the air keeps blurring the starlight. A deformable mirror makes up for these disturbances hundreds of times a second. In this way telescopes on the ground see almost as sharply as in space.
wichtigste: Adaptive optics makes up for the turbulence of the Earth’s atmosphere.
A deformable mirror constantly changes its shape to correct the light wave.
A wavefront sensor, often a Shack-Hartmann sensor, measures the distortion of the light.
The correction is adjusted hundreds to over a thousand times a second.
For an artificial guide star, a laser makes sodium atoms glow at a height of around 90 km.
Horace Babcock was the first to propose the principle, in 1953.
In eye medicine adaptive optics makes individual cells of the retina visible.

abschnitte.text: Stars twinkle because their light has to pass through the Earth’s restless air. Warm and cold layers of air are constantly mixing and bend the light slightly. For a telescope this means blurred, trembling images. Astronomers call the sharpness limited by air turbulence **seeing**. That is why even a huge telescope sees hardly more sharply than a small one without help.

First a **wavefront sensor** measures how strongly the light is distorted. A commonly used type is the **Shack-Hartmann sensor**, which works with an array of small lenses. From this a computer calculates the necessary correction at lightning speed. Then tiny actuators bend a thin, **deformable mirror** so that it exactly cancels out the distortion. This loop runs hundreds to over a thousand times a second.

To measure the distortion, you need a bright star close to the object being observed. Often there is no suitable one. That is why many observatories shoot a **laser** into the sky. It makes sodium atoms glow at a height of around 90 kilometres, creating an artificial **guide star**. At night you can see the yellowish laser beam as a fine line above the telescope.

The American astronomer **Horace Babcock** was the first to propose the principle, in 1953. At that time, however, technology was not advanced enough to manage the fast corrections. Only from the 1990s did observatories use adaptive optics regularly. Today it is used, for example, by the large telescopes of the European Southern Observatory, ESO, in Chile, of which Switzerland is also a member.

The human eye also distorts light slightly. With adaptive optics eye doctors can therefore make individual cells of the **retina** visible, for example the light-sensing cells. This helps to detect and research eye diseases early. The technique is also used in microscopes and for laser links through the air.

begriffe.erklaerung: The blurring of telescope images caused by restless air.
The shape in which a light wave spreads out, ideally completely flat.
A bright star or laser spot used to measure the distortion.
A thin mirror whose surface can be bent in a controlled way.

gewusst: With adaptive optics, telescopes on the ground can sometimes take sharper pictures than the Hubble Space Telescope.
The laser for the artificial guide star shines in the same yellow colour as old sodium street lamps.
The deformable mirror of a large telescope can be moved by more than a thousand small actuators.

teile.einleitung: Aquaplaning is when a car on a wet road suddenly floats on a film of water. The tyres then no longer have proper contact with the road. Steering and braking hardly work any more, and the car starts to slide about.
wichtigste: In aquaplaning the tyre floats up on a film of water.
It happens when the tyre tread cannot push the water away quickly enough.
The danger increases at higher speed.
Tyres with worn tread increase the risk.
A particularly large amount of water collects in ruts.
A warning sign is that the steering suddenly feels very light.
If the car starts aquaplaning, you should take your foot off the accelerator and keep the steering wheel straight.

abschnitte.text: The word comes from the Latin “aqua” for water and the English “planing” for gliding. In heavy rain a layer of water forms on the road. If a car is going too fast, the water pushes itself like a wedge under the tyre. The tyre lifts off and **floats** on the film of water. There is then hardly any **friction** between the tyre and the road.

The **tyre tread** consists of grooves and channels. They lead the water away to the side and backwards so that the tyre keeps contact with the road. A new tyre can push away several litres of water per second. If the tread is worn, it can no longer do this, and the danger of aquaplaning rises sharply. In Switzerland the tread must by law be at least **1.6 millimetres** deep, but experts recommend much more.

The faster a car goes, the less time the tyre has to lead the water away. That is why the danger increases with speed. Wide tyres and deep puddles increase the risk further. **Ruts**, dips in the road surface in which a lot of water collects, are especially dangerous.

Often the steering suddenly feels very light. Sometimes the engine briefly revs up because the wheels are spinning. The car hardly reacts to steering any more because the tyres have no grip. Anyone who notices this should not panic.

In aquaplaning you should immediately **take your foot off the accelerator** and press the clutch, or with an automatic simply stop accelerating. You keep the steering wheel straight and do not steer jerkily. Braking hard is dangerous, because otherwise the car can swerve. As soon as the tyres grip again, the car goes in the direction the wheels are pointing. The best way to prevent aquaplaning is a sensible speed in the rain and good tyres.

begriffe.erklaerung: The grooves in the tyre that lead water away and give grip.
A dip in the road surface caused by many heavy vehicles.
The force between the tyre and the road that gives grip.
How deep the grooves in the tyre still are.

gewusst: Aeroplanes can also aquaplane when landing on a wet runway.
A film of water just a few millimetres thick can be enough to make a fast car float up.
With a coin you can roughly check how deep the tyre tread still is.

teile.einleitung: In an adiabatic process a gas is compressed or expands without any heat being exchanged with its surroundings. In the process its temperature changes all by itself. This explains why a bicycle pump gets warm and why the foehn wind blows so warmly into the valley.
wichtigste: Adiabatic means that no heat is exchanged with the surroundings.
If a gas is compressed adiabatically, it warms up.
If a gas expands adiabatically, it cools down.
For an ideal gas, p·V^κ = constant.
Dry air has an adiabatic index κ of about 1.4.
Sinking dry air warms by around 1 °C per 100 metres of height.
In a p-V diagram an adiabat is steeper than an isotherm.

abschnitte.text: The word **adiabatic** comes from Greek and means roughly “not passing through”. It means that no heat passes through the walls into or out of the gas. This happens when a process runs very quickly or the gas is well insulated. The work done in compressing it then stays in the gas as **internal energy**. That is why the temperature rises.

For an **ideal gas** in adiabatic processes, p·V^κ = constant. This relationship is also called **Poisson’s equation**, after the French physicist Siméon Denis Poisson. The adiabatic index κ is about 1.4 for dry air and 5/3 for monatomic gases such as helium. If a monatomic gas at 100 kPa is compressed to half its volume, the pressure rises to around 317 kPa. In an isothermal process it would only have risen to 200 kPa, which is why the adiabat is steeper in the diagram.

If you pump up a bike tyre quickly, the bottom of the pump gets warm because the air is **compressed**. When you open a bottle of sparkling water, a fine mist often forms in the neck of the bottle. The gas expands quickly, cools down, and water vapour condenses into tiny droplets. Spray cans also get cold when you spray for a long time.

When air rises or sinks along mountains, its pressure changes and it warms or cools adiabatically. Dry air warms by around 1 °C per 100 metres as it sinks. If foehn air is 4 °C on an Alpine pass 2100 m high and sinks to 500 m in the valley, it becomes around 20 °C warm. This explains the warm **foehn**, which blows, for example, into the Reuss valley, the Hasli valley or the Rhine valley. Moist air cools more slowly as it rises, because heat is released when clouds form.

In a **diesel engine** air is compressed very quickly and strongly. If air at 300 K, that is about 27 °C, is compressed to a tenth of its volume, it reaches around 750 K, which is almost 480 °C. That is hot enough for the injected diesel fuel to ignite by itself. That is why a diesel engine does not need a spark plug. Rudolf Diesel developed this engine in the 1890s.

begriffe.erklaerung: Without exchange of heat with the surroundings.
A process in which the temperature stays the same.
Squeezing a gas into a smaller volume.
The number κ, which shows how strongly pressure and temperature react in adiabatic processes.
A warm, dry wind blowing down the side of a mountain range that faces away from the wind.

gewusst: With the foehn it can suddenly get warmer than 15 °C in the valley on a winter’s day.
With a glass fire piston you can set a piece of cotton wool alight by compressing air quickly.
Clouds often form because rising air cools adiabatically until the water vapour condenses.

teile.einleitung: The second voyage of HMS Beagle lasted from 1831 to 1836 and went all the way round the world. On board was the young naturalist Charles Darwin. What he saw and collected on the way later led him to the idea of evolution by natural selection.
wichtigste: The Beagle was a small British warship of the Royal Navy.
The captain on this voyage was Robert FitzRoy.
The main task was to survey the coasts of South America and draw sea charts.
Charles Darwin travelled as naturalist and was only 22 years old when they set off.
The voyage lasted almost five years, from December 1831 to October 1836.
On the Galápagos Islands Darwin collected birds that later turned out to be closely related species of finch.
Darwin’s travel account first appeared in 1839 under the title “Journal of Researches”.

abschnitte.text: **HMS Beagle** was a sailing ship only about 27 metres long, roughly as long as two buses one behind the other. Around 70 people lived on board in very cramped conditions. Captain **Robert FitzRoy** was himself only 26 years old. He wanted an educated companion he could talk to, and so Charles Darwin came on board.

The Beagle set off from Plymouth in England on 27 December 1831. Its main task was the **survey** of the coasts of South America, so that ships could sail more safely. In January 1832 Darwin went ashore for the first time on the Cape Verde Islands. After that came Brazil, Argentina, Tierra del Fuego, the Falkland Islands, Chile and Peru. Via the Galápagos Islands, Tahiti, New Zealand, Australia and South Africa the ship returned to England in October 1836.

Darwin spent more time on land than on the ship. In Argentina he dug up bones of extinct giant animals, for example of **giant ground sloths** such as Megatherium. On the way he read the book “Principles of Geology” by **Charles Lyell**. Lyell explained that the Earth changes through slow processes over a very long time. This idea helped Darwin to think about the slow change of living things too.

In February 1835 Darwin experienced a strong earthquake near Concepción in Chile. Afterwards he noticed that the **coast had risen**, because mussel beds were suddenly above the water. This showed him that mountain ranges such as the Andes can form bit by bit. In 1836, on the Keeling Islands in the Indian Ocean, he tested his theory on how **atolls**, ring-shaped coral islands, form.

In autumn 1835 the Beagle stayed about five weeks at the **Galápagos Islands** in the Pacific. Darwin saw giant tortoises, marine iguanas and many birds. He noticed that animals differed slightly from island to island. Only after the voyage did the ornithologist **John Gould** recognise that Darwin’s birds were closely related species of finch. Today they are called Darwin’s finches.

The travel account of 1839 made Darwin famous and is often called “The Voyage of the Beagle” today. For over 20 years Darwin thought about his observations. In 1859 he published his famous book “On the Origin of Species”. In it he explained **evolution** by natural selection, one of the most important ideas in biology.

begriffe.erklaerung: Someone who closely observes and studies animals, plants, rocks and nature.
The remains of a living thing from very long ago that have turned to stone, for example a bone.
A ring-shaped island made of coral that surrounds a lagoon in the middle.
The slow change of living things over many generations.
The precise measuring of coasts and land in order to draw maps.

gewusst: Darwin was often seasick on the ship and was therefore glad of every trip ashore.
Originally the voyage was supposed to last only about two years; in the end it was almost five.
At first Darwin did not label his finches on the Galápagos Islands carefully by island, which he later regretted.

teile.einleitung: Anders Celsius was a Swedish astronomer who lived almost 300 years ago. The temperature scale in degrees Celsius that we use every day is named after him. The astonishing thing is that his scale was exactly the other way round at first.
wichtigste: Anders Celsius was above all an astronomer, a scientist who studies the stars.
He lived from 1701 to 1744 and was only about 42 years old when he died.
He worked in the Swedish university town of Uppsala.
In 1742 he presented his temperature scale.
Originally the scale was the other way round: water boiled at 0 and froze at 100 degrees.
He studied the northern lights and linked them to the Earth’s magnetic field.
In 1736 he took part in the Lapland expedition to measure the Earth.

abschnitte.text: Anders Celsius was born in 1701 in **Uppsala** in Sweden and died there in 1744. He came from a family of scholars; his father and grandfather had both been professors. Celsius himself became professor of **astronomy** at Uppsala University. He also travelled through Europe, for example to Germany, Italy, France and England, to get to know other scientists and observatories.

In 1742 Celsius proposed a temperature scale with two fixed points: the **freezing point** and the **boiling point** of water. He divided the gap between them into 100 equal parts. In his version, however, the boiling point was at 0 degrees and the freezing point at 100 degrees. Only after his death was the scale turned round, so that water today freezes at 0 degrees and boils at 100 degrees. Another important discovery of his was that the boiling point depends on the air pressure.

In 1736 Celsius travelled with a French expedition under Pierre Louis Moreau de Maupertuis to **Lapland** in the far north. There the researchers measured how long one degree is along a meridian of the Earth. The result showed that the Earth is slightly **flattened** at the poles, so not perfectly round. In this way they confirmed a prediction by Isaac Newton.

Celsius closely observed the **northern lights** in the sky over Sweden. Together with his assistant Olof Hiorter he noticed that compass needles trembled restlessly when northern lights were shining. In this way they recognised a connection between the northern lights and the Earth’s **magnetic field**. Celsius also made sure that Uppsala got a modern observatory, which was finished in 1741.

The Celsius scale is used today in almost every country in the world, including Switzerland. Only a few countries such as the USA still use degrees Fahrenheit in everyday life. In science people often calculate in **kelvin**, where a step of 1 kelvin is exactly the same size as 1 degree Celsius. A crater on the Moon and a minor planet also bear the name Celsius.

begriffe.erklaerung: A scientist who studies stars, planets and the sky.
The temperature at which water turns to ice, today 0 degrees Celsius.
The temperature at which water boils, about 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.
Glowing bands of colour in the night sky, mainly in the far north and south.

gewusst: On the original Celsius scale, a hot summer’s day of 30 degrees today would have been a day of 70 degrees.
Celsius died of tuberculosis at only about 42, before his scale became world-famous.
A temperature difference of 1 degree Celsius is exactly the same size as 1 kelvin.

teile.einleitung: A zoonosis is an infectious disease that can be passed between animals and humans. Many well-known diseases originally came from animals, for example rabies or the plague. That is why experts today look at the health of humans, animals and the environment together.
wichtigste: A zoonosis is an infectious disease that is passed between animals and humans.
According to frequently quoted estimates, around 60 per cent of the known infectious diseases of humans are zoonotic in origin.
In Switzerland, rabies was fought with vaccine baits for foxes.
The fox tapeworm is passed on through eggs in fox droppings and can seriously damage the liver.
In Switzerland, ticks transmit tick-borne encephalitis.
The plague was caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and was passed from rats to humans by fleas.
The “One Health” approach looks at humans, animals and the environment together.

abschnitte.text: The word **zoonosis** comes from Greek and means roughly “animal disease”. It refers to diseases whose pathogens jump from animals to humans or the other way round. Pathogens can be viruses, bacteria, fungi or parasites. The term was coined in the 19th century by the German doctor Rudolf Virchow. According to frequently quoted estimates, around 60 per cent of the known infectious diseases of humans originally came from animals.

Some pathogens enter the body through a **bite** or scratch, as with rabies. Others are transmitted by insects or ticks that first bite an animal and then a human. Such carriers are called **vectors**. You can also become infected through contaminated food, for example undercooked poultry containing salmonella. Still other pathogens, such as the eggs of the fox tapeworm, get into the environment through droppings.

In Switzerland the **tick** transmits tick-borne encephalitis, TBE for short, and Lyme disease. There is a vaccine against TBE that is recommended for almost all of Switzerland. The **fox tapeworm** is a parasite whose eggs are found in fox droppings and which can seriously damage the human liver. **Rabies** was fought from 1978 onwards by laying out vaccine baits for foxes, and Switzerland was a pioneer in this. Since 1999 Switzerland has been considered free of rabies in land animals.

The **plague** is one of the best-known zoonoses. It is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis, which fleas carried from rats to humans. In the 14th century the “Black Death” killed about a third of Europe’s population. More recent diseases such as bird flu also come from animals. **Bats** are considered an important natural reservoir for many coronaviruses and lyssaviruses.

Because humans, animals and the environment are closely connected, doctors, vets and environmental experts work together in the **One Health** approach. They monitor diseases in wild and farm animals in order to spot new dangers early. If you want to do something yourself, wash your hands thoroughly after touching animals. After trips to woods and meadows you should check yourself for ticks. Meat and eggs should be cooked thoroughly, and you should not touch dead or unusually tame wild animals.

begriffe.erklaerung: A disease that can be passed between animals and humans.
A tiny living thing or virus that causes a disease.
An animal, such as a tick or mosquito, that carries a pathogen on to others.
Animals in which a pathogen lives permanently, often without making them ill.
An approach that looks at the health of humans, animals and the environment together.

gewusst: In 1978 Switzerland was the first country to test vaccine baits for foxes in the wild.
Humans can also infect animals, for example great apes with cold viruses.
Ticks lie in wait in grass and bushes and get brushed off onto you; they do not jump down from trees.

teile.einleitung: The ampere is the unit of electric current. It tells you how much electric charge flows through a wire per second. It is named after the French physicist André-Marie Ampère.
wichtigste: The ampere is the unit of electric current.
The unit symbol is A, and the current itself is abbreviated as I.
It is one of the seven base units of the International System of Units, SI.
It is named after the Frenchman André-Marie Ampère, who lived from 1775 to 1836.
Current is measured with an ammeter.
Current times voltage gives the electrical power in watts.
Even small currents through the body can be life-threatening.

abschnitte.text: Electric current is the flow of electrically charged particles, in metal wires the flow of **electrons**. The **current** tells you how much charge flows through the conductor per second. You can compare it with water in a pipe: the current corresponds to the amount of water that flows through per second. With 1 ampere, around 6 quintillion electrons flow through the wire every second.

**André-Marie Ampère** was a French physicist and mathematician. Around 1820 he studied how electric currents produce magnetic forces. He showed that two parallel wires attract each other when current flows through them in the same direction. In doing so he laid one of the foundations of electrodynamics. In his honour the unit of current was named after him in 1881.

The ampere is one of the seven **base units** of the International System of Units, together with the metre, kilogram, second, kelvin, mole and candela. Since 2019 it has been defined using the electric charge of a single electron. Smaller currents are given in milliamperes; a milliampere is a thousandth of an ampere. Together with the **voltage** in volts, the current gives the power in watts.

A small light-emitting diode needs only about 20 milliamperes. A 2000-watt kettle on the Swiss mains at 230 volts draws just under 9 amperes. In Swiss homes the circuits are usually protected by **fuses** of 10 to 16 amperes. If more current is drawn, the fuse switches off so that the wires do not get too hot. A lightning bolt, on the other hand, often reaches tens of thousands of amperes.

If current flows through the human body, it can throw the muscles and the heart out of rhythm. Even a few hundredths of an ampere can be life-threatening. That is why you must never fiddle with sockets or damaged cables. A **residual current device**, or RCD for short, switches off the power in a fraction of a second if something is wrong. Railway power lines are especially dangerous, and you must never get too close to them.

begriffe.erklaerung: The amount of electric charge that flows through a conductor per second.
A tiny, negatively charged particle that forms the current in a wire.
A basic unit of measurement from which other units are derived.
A safety switch that cuts off the current if it gets too high.

gewusst: The unit ampere was fixed in 1881 at an international congress of electricians in Paris.
An electric eel can produce electric shocks of about one ampere.
The unit symbol A is written without the accent, even though Ampère has an accent in his name.

teile.einleitung: The cytoplasm is the entire contents of a cell inside the cell membrane, except for the nucleus. It consists of a jelly-like fluid and many tiny cell parts. Many vital processes of the cell take place here.
wichtigste: The cytoplasm includes everything inside the cell membrane except the nucleus.
The fluid basic substance without the organelles is called cytosol.
Organelles are small cell parts with particular tasks.
The cytoskeleton is a network of protein fibres that supports the cell from the inside.
The endoplasmic reticulum is a system of channels made of membranes that transports substances.
Glycolysis, the first step in breaking down sugar, takes place in the cytoplasm.
In the leaves of waterweed you can see cytoplasmic streaming under the microscope.

abschnitte.text: The word **cytoplasm** comes from Greek and means roughly “cell formation”. It refers to the whole contents of a cell between the cell membrane and the nucleus. It consists of the basic fluid, the **cytosol**, and the **organelles** lying in it. In bacteria, which have no nucleus, the genetic material also lies directly in the cytoplasm.

The **cytosol** consists mostly of water. Salts, sugars, amino acids and a great many proteins are dissolved in it. That is why it is not runny like water but rather thick like a gel. Countless **enzymes** work in the cytosol, speeding up chemical reactions.

Many **organelles** lie in the cytoplasm, and they can be compared with the organs of the body. The mitochondria produce energy, and the ribosomes assemble proteins. The **endoplasmic reticulum** is a system of channels made of membranes that makes and transports substances. Plant cells also contain chloroplasts for photosynthesis and a large vacuole.

A network of fine protein fibres, the **cytoskeleton**, runs through the cytoplasm. It supports the cell from the inside, rather like tent poles support a tent. It also serves as a network of rails on which small vesicles and organelles are transported. During cell division it helps to share out the genetic material fairly between the two daughter cells.

The cytoplasm is constantly moving. In the leaf cells of **waterweed** you can watch under a light microscope how the green chloroplasts travel in a circle; this is called **cytoplasmic streaming**. The breakdown of sugar to obtain energy, **glycolysis**, also begins in the cytoplasm. The further steps then take place in the mitochondria.

begriffe.erklaerung: The fluid basic substance of the cytoplasm without the organelles.
A small cell part with a particular task.
A network of protein fibres that supports the cell and makes transport possible.
The first step in breaking down sugar to obtain energy.
The movement of the cell contents, which can be seen under the microscope.

gewusst: A single cell can contain millions of ribosomes in its cytoplasm.
Cytoplasmic streaming in plant cells gets faster if you shine a lamp on the cells or warm them slightly.
Human red blood cells have no nucleus at all and consist almost entirely of cytoplasm full of blood pigment.

teile.einleitung: Alpine solar plants are large photovoltaic installations built high up in the mountains. There the sun often shines above the fog even in winter, and the snow reflects extra light onto the panels. Switzerland is relying on such plants to produce more electricity for the winter.
wichtigste: Alpine solar plants supply much more winter electricity than installations on the Swiss Plateau.
Snow reflects a lot of sunlight onto the panels and increases production.
Bifacial panels use the light on both the front and the back.
Cold makes the efficiency of solar cells rise.
The panels are often mounted very steeply so that snow slides off and the low winter sun is used well.
One of the first large alpine plants was built on the dam wall of the Muttsee in the canton of Glarus.
With the Solarexpress, Parliament decided in 2022 on temporary support for large alpine plants.

abschnitte.text: An **alpine solar plant** is a photovoltaic installation in the mountains, usually at over 1500 metres. It turns sunlight directly into electricity with **solar panels**. Some stand on open mountain meadows, others on dam walls or on avalanche barriers. In Switzerland they are regarded as an important building block of the energy transition.

On the Swiss Plateau high fog often lies for weeks in winter, and solar installations then supply little electricity. In the mountains the sun often shines above the **sea of fog**. In addition, the white snow reflects a lot of light; this reflectivity is called **albedo**. That is why alpine plants supply much more winter electricity. It is precisely in winter that Switzerland needs a particularly large amount of electricity and so far has had to import some of it.

Many alpine plants use **bifacial panels**, which catch light on both the front and the back. In this way the light reflected by the snow is also used. The panels are often mounted very steeply or even vertically. Then the snow slides off, and the low winter sun hits the surface well. In addition, the **efficiency** of solar cells rises in the cold, because they work better when cool.

One of Switzerland’s first large alpine solar plants was built on the dam wall of the **Muttsee** in the canton of Glarus. It lies at a height of around 2500 metres and was completed in 2022. Around 5000 panels hang there on the wall and together have an output of about 2.2 megawatts. The project is called AlpinSolar and was built by the energy companies Axpo and IWB.

In 2022 the Federal Parliament decided on temporary support for large alpine solar plants, the **Solarexpress**. After that many projects were planned, for example in Valais and the Grisons. Some, however, were rejected by the municipalities or made smaller. Critics fear that the landscape and nature will suffer, and building in the mountains is expensive. Supporters stress that Switzerland urgently needs more winter electricity.

How much power a plant supplies depends on its area, the solar radiation and its efficiency. You multiply the panel area by the radiation and the efficiency. With an area of 1000 m², radiation of 1000 W/m² and an efficiency of 20 per cent, this gives 200 kW. How much electricity is produced over the year also depends on the weather and the position of the sun.

begriffe.erklaerung: The direct conversion of sunlight into electricity.
A solar panel that turns light into electricity on both sides.
How strongly a surface reflects light; snow reflects a great deal.
Electricity produced in the winter half of the year, when demand is high.
What percentage of the incoming energy is turned into electricity.

gewusst: Solar cells work better in the cold than in the heat.
The plant at the Muttsee hangs vertically on a dam wall so that no snow settles on it.
Above the sea of fog the sun often shines for hours in winter while it is grey on the Swiss Plateau.

teile.einleitung: Science is the search for knowledge about the world using precise methods that can be checked. It explains, for example, why an apple falls from a tree or why water boils at 100 degrees. This chapter is about researchers, measuring instruments, laws of nature, substances, space and life.
wichtigste: Science searches for knowledge using methods that can be checked.
An apple falls down because of gravity.
At sea level water boils at 100 degrees Celsius.
The natural sciences include physics, chemistry, biology and astronomy.
Measuring instruments such as thermometers, microscopes and telescopes make the invisible visible.
Researchers test their ideas with observations and experiments.
With ETH, EPFL and CERN, Switzerland is an important place for research.

abschnitte.text: In German the word for **science** means “creating knowledge”, and doing so in a careful way that can be checked. Researchers ask questions, observe, measure and carry out experiments. What they find out is published and checked by others. In this way an ever more accurate picture of the world gradually builds up.

**Physics** studies forces, energy, light and motion. **Chemistry** investigates substances and how they change, for example water with the formula H₂O. Biology deals with living things, from the cell to the elephant. Astronomy looks out into space, and geology studies the Earth and its rocks.

Why does an apple fall down from a tree? The answer is **gravity**, with which the Earth pulls everything towards itself. In 1687 the English scientist Isaac Newton described the law of gravitation in his famous book. According to a well-known story, a falling apple is said to have given him the idea. The same force also keeps the Moon in its orbit round the Earth.

At sea level water boils at 100 degrees Celsius and freezes at 0 degrees. Anders Celsius used these two points for his **temperature scale** in 1742. In the mountains the air pressure is lower, so water boils there at lower temperatures. Fixed values like these make experiments comparable, no matter where in the world they take place.

With the **microscope** we see tiny cells and bacteria, and with the telescope distant stars and galaxies. Thermometers, voltmeters and seismographs measure temperature, voltage and earthquakes. Computers help to analyse huge amounts of data. Many discoveries only became possible once a new measuring instrument had been invented.

Switzerland is one of the strongest countries in the world for research. **ETH Zurich** was founded in 1855, and many Nobel Prize winners have studied or taught there. Albert Einstein published ground-breaking papers in Bern in 1905. At **CERN** near Geneva, founded in 1954, the World Wide Web was even invented in 1989.

begriffe.erklaerung: A rule according to which processes in nature always happen in the same way.
A planned test used to check an idea.
The force with which bodies attract each other, for example the Earth an apple.
A reasoned guess that can be tested.

gewusst: On the Moon gravity is about six times weaker than on Earth, so you can jump much higher there.
On the summit of Mount Everest water boils at only around 70 degrees Celsius.
At CERN near Geneva is the LHC, the largest particle accelerator in the world; its ring is 27 kilometres long.

teile.einleitung: The general theory of relativity is Albert Einstein’s theory of gravity from 1915. It explains gravitation not as an ordinary force but as the curving of space and time by masses. Without it, GPS devices would show wrong positions.
wichtigste: Albert Einstein published the general theory of relativity in 1915.
Masses curve space and time, and we feel this curvature as gravity.
According to the equivalence principle, gravity and acceleration cannot be told apart locally.
Clocks run more slowly in strong gravitational fields, so a little more slowly at sea level than on a high mountain.
Large masses bend light and can act as gravitational lenses.
The Swiss mathematician Marcel Grossmann helped Einstein with differential geometry.
The theory predicts black holes and gravitational waves.

abschnitte.text: Einstein imagined standing in a lift without windows. You could not tell whether the lift was standing on Earth or accelerating steadily upwards in space. This idea is called the **equivalence principle**. From it Einstein concluded that gravity is a property of **spacetime**. A popular comparison is a heavy ball on a stretched sheet: it makes a dip, and smaller balls roll towards it.

Einstein studied at ETH Zurich and worked at the patent office in Bern from 1902 to 1909. There, in 1905, he developed the special theory of relativity. For the general theory he needed difficult mathematics. His friend from his student days, **Marcel Grossmann**, professor of mathematics at ETH, showed him the differential geometry he needed. In November 1915, in Berlin, Einstein presented his finished **field equations**. On one side they have the curvature of spacetime, on the other side, as its source, the energy-momentum tensor.

The first thing the theory explained was a small deviation in the orbit of the planet **Mercury**. In 1919 British researchers observed during a solar eclipse that starlight passing close to the sun is bent, as Einstein had predicted. Today we see **gravitational lenses**: large clusters of galaxies bend the light of galaxies behind them and show them distorted as arcs. Radar signals that travel close past the sun to a planet and back take a little longer than they would without the sun.

The theory says that time passes more slowly in strong gravitational fields. A clock at sea level therefore runs a little more slowly than a clock on a high mountain. Light travelling outwards from a strong gravitational field is **redshifted**. Around 1960 the Pound-Rebka experiment measured this redshift with gamma rays in a tower at Harvard University. GPS satellites have to take these effects into account; otherwise positions would be wrong by kilometres every day.

The theory leads to **black holes**, from which not even light can escape. In 2019 the Event Horizon Telescope showed the first image of the shadow of a black hole. In 2015 **gravitational waves** were measured for the first time, tiny ripples in spacetime from two black holes merging. The Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded for this in 2017.

Einstein also applied the theory to the whole universe. In 1917 he added the **cosmological constant** so that a static universe was possible. Later it turned out that the universe is expanding. Today such a constant is used again to describe the accelerating expansion of the universe. The general theory of relativity is therefore the basis of modern cosmology.

begriffe.erklaerung: Space and time thought of together as one four-dimensional structure.
The insight that gravity and acceleration feel the same on a small scale.
A large mass that bends light like a magnifying glass.
Light is shifted to longer wavelengths, that is, made redder.
Tiny ripples in spacetime that spread out at the speed of light.

gewusst: Einstein did not receive his Nobel Prize for the theory of relativity, but for explaining the photoelectric effect.
Because gravity is weaker up there, the clocks in GPS satellites run around 45 millionths of a second fast every day, which has to be corrected.
The first gravitational waves ever measured came from more than a billion light years away.

teile.einleitung: In physics, absorption means that a substance takes in light, heat radiation or sound and, so to speak, swallows it. A red apple, for example, looks red because it reflects red light and swallows the other colours. The energy taken in does not disappear, but is usually turned into heat.
wichtigste: Absorption means taking in or swallowing radiation or sound.
A red apple reflects red light and swallows the other colours.
The opposite of absorption is reflection, throwing back.
The absorbed energy is usually turned into heat.
Black objects swallow almost all light and get especially warm in the sun.
Plants absorb red and blue light and therefore look green.
Sound can also be absorbed, for example by curtains or foam.

abschnitte.text: White sunlight is a mixture of all the colours of the rainbow. When it hits an object, some of the colours are **absorbed** and some are **reflected**. We only see the colours that are thrown back into our eyes. A red apple swallows green and blue and reflects red. A white sheet of paper reflects all colours, while a black T-shirt swallows almost all of them.

When a substance absorbs light, it takes in its **energy**. This energy makes the particles of the substance move more strongly, and it gets warmer. That is why a black car heats up much more in the sun than a white one. In summer people therefore like to wear light-coloured clothes. **Solar collectors** on house roofs are dark so that they take in as much of the sun’s heat as possible.

Plants contain the green pigment **chlorophyll**. It mainly absorbs red and blue light and uses the energy for photosynthesis. Green light is reflected, which is why leaves look green. The **ozone layer** in the atmosphere absorbs a large part of the sun’s dangerous UV radiation. Without it, life on land would hardly be possible.

**Sound waves** can also be absorbed. Soft and porous materials such as carpets, curtains, upholstered furniture or foam swallow sound especially well. That is why special wall panels are fitted in recording studios and concert halls. In an empty room with bare walls, on the other hand, there is a strong echo. Fresh snow also swallows a lot of sound, which is why a snowy landscape seems so quiet.

**Sunglasses** absorb part of the visible light and above all UV rays, which can damage the eyes. Sun cream contains substances that swallow or reflect UV radiation. In a microwave oven the water in the food absorbs the microwaves and gets hot. Researchers use the absorption of light to measure which substances a sample contains.

begriffe.erklaerung: The taking in of light, heat radiation or sound by a substance.
The throwing back of light or sound at a surface.
A green pigment in plants that takes in light for photosynthesis.
A layer in the atmosphere that swallows harmful UV radiation.

gewusst: The blackest artificial material swallows over 99.9 per cent of light and makes objects look like flat holes.
The sky is blue because the air scatters blue light more strongly than red.
Glacier ice looks blue because thick ice absorbs red light a little more strongly than blue.

teile.einleitung: The adiabatic lapse rate describes how strongly a rising or sinking parcel of air cools down or warms up. Dry air cools by about 1 degree per 100 metres as it rises, while moist, saturated air cools more slowly. With this knowledge you can explain clouds, thunderstorms and the foehn in the Alps.
wichtigste: “Adiabatic” means that a parcel of air exchanges no heat with its surroundings.
When air rises, it expands because of the falling air pressure and cools down in the process.
Dry air cools by about 1 °C per 100 metres; this is the dry adiabatic lapse rate.
Saturated air cools more slowly, because heat is released when water vapour condenses.
At the height of the condensation level the air becomes saturated and clouds form.
The dry adiabatic lapse rate comes from the acceleration due to gravity and the specific heat capacity of air.
A layer of air in which the temperature rises with height is called an inversion.

abschnitte.text: Meteorologists often imagine an **air parcel**, a kind of invisible balloon of air that rises or sinks. **Adiabatic** means that this parcel exchanges no heat with its surroundings as it moves. Even so, its temperature changes, because the pressure changes. If it rises, it expands and cools; if it sinks, it is squeezed together and warms up, rather like a bicycle pump gets warm when you pump.

For dry air the cooling is around 1 °C per 100 metres; this is the **dry adiabatic lapse rate**. It comes from the acceleration due to gravity divided by the specific heat capacity of air. If a dry air parcel rises, for example, from 500 to 2500 metres, it cools from 20 °C to 0 °C. Saturated air, on the other hand, only cools by about 0.4 to 0.7 °C per 100 metres; this is the **moist adiabatic lapse rate**.

As it rises, the air keeps cooling until it cannot hold any more water vapour. This height is called the **condensation level**, and the first cloud droplets form there. You can see this height directly in the sky at the flat bottom of heap clouds. When water vapour condenses, heat is released, so the air then cools more slowly and can rise further, sometimes into a tall thundercloud.

Whether air rises depends on how quickly the temperature of the surroundings falls with height. If it falls more slowly than the moist adiabatic rate, a rising air parcel soon becomes colder than its surroundings and sinks back; the layering is **absolutely stable**. If it falls faster, the air keeps on rising; the layering is unstable and thunderstorms can form. In an **inversion** it even gets warmer with height, as with the high fog over the Swiss Plateau in winter.

A well-known example is the **foehn** in the Alps. With a south foehn, moist air rises on the southern side of the Alps, cools first at the dry and then at the moist adiabatic rate, and loses its moisture as rain over Ticino. On the northern side the now dry air sinks and warms by around 1 °C per 100 metres. That is why it arrives in valleys such as the Reuss valley near Altdorf or the Rhine valley much warmer than it was at the same height in the south.

begriffe.erklaerung: An imagined amount of air whose path and temperature are followed.
Without exchange of heat with the surroundings.
The height at which rising air is saturated and clouds form.
A layer of air in which the temperature rises with height instead of falling.
A warm, dry wind blowing down the sheltered side of a mountain range.

gewusst: The flat bottoms of fair-weather clouds, all at the same height, show exactly where the condensation level is.
With a strong foehn, the northern edge of the Alps can suddenly feel as warm as spring in winter.
On average the temperature in the atmosphere falls by about 0.65 °C per 100 metres, which is less than the dry adiabatic rate.

teile.einleitung: A hydrometer is a measuring instrument used to find the density of a liquid. It looks like a glass thermometer with a thick, weighted bulb and floats upright in the liquid. Depending on how deep it sinks, you can read off the density on a scale.
wichtigste: A hydrometer measures the density of liquids.
In German it is also known as a “sinking spindle”.
In a liquid with a higher density it sinks less deeply.
That is why the larger density values are at the bottom of the scale.
A weighted bulb at the bottom, for example with lead shot, makes it float upright.
Winemakers use it to measure the must weight in degrees Oechsle.
An alcoholmeter is a hydrometer that shows the alcohol content.

abschnitte.text: The **hydrometer** is a floating measuring instrument made of glass. At the top it has a thin neck with a scale, and at the bottom a thick body with a weight. In German it is also called a **sinking spindle**. The weight, often lead shot, makes it float upright and steadily in the liquid.

The hydrometer uses **buoyancy**, which Archimedes already described in ancient times. A floating body sinks until it pushes aside as much liquid as it weighs itself. In a liquid with a high **density** it does not need to sink as deep to do this. That is why the hydrometer sticks out further in dense liquids. The larger density values are therefore at the bottom of the stem, and the smaller ones at the top.

At the grape harvest, winemakers measure how much sugar there is in the grape juice. The more sugar, the higher the density of the must. In Switzerland the **must weight** is given in **degrees Oechsle**. A must of 80 degrees Oechsle, for example, has a density of 1.080 g/cm³. The unit is named after the German inventor Ferdinand Oechsle from Pforzheim.

An **alcoholmeter** is a hydrometer that shows the alcohol content of a mixture of water and alcohol. This works because alcohol has a lower density than water. In the past hydrometers were also used to check how well charged the lead-acid batteries in cars were. The fuller the battery, the denser the acid inside it. The density of milk, sea water or antifreeze can also be measured in this way.

The idea is very old. As early as around the year 400, the Greek scholar Synesius of Cyrene described such an instrument in a letter to the mathematician **Hypatia**. Later it was improved again and again and given various scales. Today there are also electronic density meters, but the simple hydrometer is cheap and needs no electricity.

begriffe.erklaerung: How much mass there is in a certain volume, for example in grams per cubic centimetre.
The force with which a liquid pushes an object in it upwards.
A unit for the must weight of grape juice.
Another name for the hydrometer in German.

gewusst: In salty sea water a hydrometer floats higher than in fresh water.
The number in degrees Oechsle corresponds to the decimal places of the density: 80 degrees means 1.080 g/cm³.
Home brewers also use a hydrometer to measure how much of the sugar in their beer has already fermented.

teile.einleitung: Absolute zero is the lowest temperature that can exist at all. It is 0 kelvin, which is minus 273.15 degrees Celsius. It cannot get colder, and it can never be reached exactly either.
wichtigste: Absolute zero is 0 kelvin or minus 273.15 degrees Celsius.
In Fahrenheit it corresponds to minus 459.67 degrees.
As a substance approaches absolute zero, the movement of its particles becomes almost zero.
In the laboratory you can only get very close to absolute zero, but never reach it exactly.
A temperature of minus 300 degrees Celsius is physically impossible.
The background radiation in space is only about 2.7 kelvin warm.
At normal pressure helium stays liquid even close to absolute zero.

abschnitte.text: **Temperature** is a measure of how strongly the smallest particles of a substance are moving. The colder a substance is, the more slowly its atoms and molecules jiggle. At **absolute zero** this movement would be as small as the laws of nature allow at all. That is why nothing can be colder. A temperature of minus 300 degrees Celsius is therefore impossible.

Scientists measure low temperatures in **kelvin**, abbreviated K. The scale starts at absolute zero, so there are no negative kelvin values. One kelvin step is the same size as one degree Celsius. That is why 0 K corresponds exactly to minus 273.15 degrees Celsius, and water freezes at about 273 K. The unit is named after the British physicist William Thomson, who was later called **Lord Kelvin** and proposed an absolute temperature scale in 1848.

Back in the 18th and 19th centuries researchers observed that a **gas** gets smaller and smaller as it cools at constant pressure. For each degree of cooling it shrinks by about one 273rd of its volume at 0 degrees Celsius. If you carry on calculating, the volume would become zero at about minus 273 degrees. This led to the idea of a lowest possible temperature. Real gases, however, turn liquid or solid before that.

A law of nature, the **third law of thermodynamics**, says that absolute zero can never be reached completely. With laser cooling and other tricks, however, researchers have got within tiny fractions of a kelvin. In 1995 they used this to create the first **Bose-Einstein condensate**, a special state of matter in which many atoms behave like a single giant atom. At normal pressure helium even stays liquid close to absolute zero and below about 2.2 kelvin it can flow without any friction. This state is called superfluidity.

Even space is not quite that cold: the **background radiation** from the early days of the universe is about 2.7 kelvin. Some substances conduct electricity with no resistance at all at very low temperatures; this is called **superconductivity**. At CERN near Geneva the magnets of the large particle accelerator LHC are cooled to about 1.9 kelvin so that they become superconducting. MRI scanners in hospitals also use superconducting magnets cooled with liquid helium. Quantum computers also work at temperatures just above absolute zero.

begriffe.erklaerung: The unit of temperature that starts at absolute zero.
When a substance conducts electricity with no resistance at all in great cold.
A state of matter in which ultra-cold atoms behave like a single particle.
Weak radiation from the early days of the universe that fills the whole of space.

gewusst: The magnets of the LHC at CERN are colder than empty space.
The Nobel Prize in Physics was awarded in 2001 for making the first Bose-Einstein condensate.
At normal pressure helium does not become solid even at absolute zero; that also needs high pressure.

teile.einleitung: Repulsion is a force that pushes two things away from each other. You can feel it when you try to press two magnets together with the same poles facing. Electrically charged objects can also repel each other.
wichtigste: Like magnetic poles repel each other: north pole and north pole, or south pole and south pole.
Unlike poles attract each other, which is the opposite of repulsion.
Repulsion works even before two magnets touch.
If you turn one of the magnets round, they attract instead of repelling each other.
An iron nail is never repelled by a magnet, only attracted.
Only another magnet can repel a magnet, which is how you can be sure something is a magnet.
Like electric charges also repel each other.

abschnitte.text: In **repulsion** two objects push each other away without anyone touching them. With magnets this happens when **like poles** face each other. The closer the magnets get, the stronger the force becomes. You feel a soft, invisible resistance like a cushion of air.

Every magnet has a **north pole** and a **south pole**. If a pole repels the north pole of another magnet, it is itself a north pole. Two magnets that repel each other attract as soon as you turn one round. Iron, nickel and cobalt are attracted, but never repelled. That is why repulsion is the reliable test of whether an object is itself a magnet.

If you put several **ring magnets** on a rod with like poles facing each other, some of them float in the air. Repulsion holds them up against gravity. If you press the top magnet down and let go, it springs back up like a spring. The more magnets there are on top, the closer together the lower ones move.

Electric charges can also repel each other. If you rub a balloon on your hair, the hairs all get the same charge. Because **like charges** repel each other, the hairs then stick out in all directions. Positive and negative charges, on the other hand, attract each other. In atomic nuclei the positively charged protons also repel each other.

Some **maglev trains** use magnetic forces so that the train floats above the track without wheels. In Japan such a train floats several centimetres above the guideway thanks to very strong magnets. Magnetic bearings in machines also use magnetic forces so that parts turn almost without friction. In everyday life you find repulsion in magnetic toys and in experiments at school.

begriffe.erklaerung: One of the two places on a magnet where the force is strongest.
The pole of a magnet that points to geographic north when the magnet can turn freely.
The opposite of repulsion: things move towards each other.
A property of particles that can be positive or negative.

gewusst: The repulsion of two magnets also works through paper, wood and water.
If you break a magnet into two pieces, each piece again has a north and a south pole.
Without the electric repulsion of electrons you could fall through a chair onto the floor.
